report.title: How efficient the life kernel is: per-life cost, profile, exact speedups and cross-machine bitwise risk (CATCH test bodies, loaded laptop)

findings.claim: One life of an evolved CATCH body costs 0.07 to 0.15 CPU-s at T=1024 on one E-core. The cost is linear in cell-time, at 1.2 to 1.5 us per cell-time unit (1.1 to 1.8 us per ledger event), whatever T is. These figures are for a loaded machine, so they are pessimistic.
findings.evidence:
bench.py, prod build, threads=1, one life per call, pinned to E-cores 4-11 at nice 19; CPU is the C call's thread CPU time. T=1024, 32 lives per body:
- speck_s5: 0.150 s (p10-p90 0.128-0.173), 97k events, 118k cell-units, 5.6k spikes, n_end 122, 1.27 us per cell-unit
- speck_s0: 0.074 s, 41k events, 56k cell-units, n_end 143, 1.32 us
- lmax4_s5: 0.118 s, 104k events, 82k cell-units, 9.6k spikes, n_end 85, 1.44 us
T sweep (768 and 1536, 16 lives each): us per cell-unit stays within 5% of the T=1024 value. speck_s0 keeps growing (86 cells at T=768, 290 at T=1536, 0.224 s per life).
The 32 parents in each run's population.json (2 lives each) cost the same: 0.154, 0.068 and 0.108 s per life.
The pilot's own curves agree: t_eval*3/(768*pop_body*T) gives a median of 1.40-1.56 wall-us per cell-unit per thread. t_gen ≈ t_eval + t_recheck, and the Python remainder has a median of 0 s.
Load bias: CPU time is inflated by L2/L3 shared with pilot threads and by the 15 W chip's lower all-core clock. Wall/CPU ran 1.0-3.4, so wall times mean nothing here.
Files: raw/bench_prod.jsonl, raw/analyse_bench.txt, raw/summary.json.

findings.claim: The scheduler handles about 2x as many events as the ledger's 'events' column counts, at 590-730 ns each. Receptor candidates make up 43-60% of all heap events, and in SPECK only about 4% of them are accepted.
findings.evidence:
counts.py: counting build, 16 lives per body. Its hashes equal the production build's.
- Heap pops per life: 206k, 108k and 189k, against ledger events of 93k, 41k and 99k.
- speck_s5 mix: receptor candidates 54%, ticks 28%, spike arrivals 15%, receptor deliveries 2%, notices and claims under 1%.
- Acceptance (bench ledger): 4.4% (speck_s5), 4.1% (speck_s0), 19.7% (lmax4_s5, sigma 1.5).
- Per heap event: 2.2-2.7 records (R_PACKET is 58% of all records), 5.5-6.8 libm calls (about 1.18M exp, 112k log and 117k tanh per speck_s5 life, roughly 20 exp per tick), 2.06e5 heap pushes, at most 445 entries in the heap.
Files: raw/counts.jsonl, raw/analyse_bench.txt.

findings.claim: Cost model: CPU per life ≈ 187 ns per heap event + 1.9 us per GRN tick (R2 0.992). In ledger terms that is about 1.17 us per cell-unit + 2.0 us per spike (R2 0.98), or 0.58 us per cell-unit + 2.4 us per spike + 0.60 us per receptor candidate (R2 0.99). Ticks run at about 0.5 per cell-unit.
findings.evidence:
Least squares in analyse_bench.py.
- Count fit: 48 lives (counting build counts against production timings).
- Ledger fit: 144 lives (3 bodies x 3 values of T).
- Fitted on one E-core under load.
Planning example: a 126-cell population needs about 1,070 lives per generation (256x3 selection + 64x4 recheck + about 5% for the rounds every 10 generations). At mean T 1109 that is about 175 E-core CPU-s per generation, or about 24 CPU-h per 500 generations.

findings.claim:
Where the time goes (exclusive cost centres, libm time charged to its caller), the same within 2 points for all 3 bodies:
- event queue (binary heap) 14-16%
- phenotype readout 23x16 + decode 12-13%
- chemistry inbox and per-neighbour packet sends 9-11%
- GRN regulation 16x25 + sigma 9-10%
- hash folding 9.7-10%
- record emission and zeroing 8.2-8.6%
- receptor thinning (halo, dot position) 5.5-6.7%
- batch dispatch 4.8-6.2%
- receptor candidate scheduling (log + hash) 3.9-5.2%
- membrane 3.7-5.9%
- accountant sums and flight queue 3.2-3.6%
- derive 2.8-3.2%
- record sort/flush 1.6-1.9%
- scheduler loop about 1%
- allocation about 1%, almost all of it the inlined capacity check
- site map 0.3%
libm is 19% of the total: exp about 14% (GRN sigma 7.0%, halo 1.75%, dot_gain 1.7%, traces 1.6%, vnow 1.1%, chemistry decay 0.9%), log 2.3%, tanh 2.1%, nearbyint/floor 0.5%.
findings.evidence:
perf was not usable: there is no perf binary for kernel 6.17.0-1032-oem and perf_event_paranoid is 4. I wrote a SIGPROF sampler instead (prof.c: ITIMER_PROF at 1 kHz of CPU time, backtrace through the signal frame) and resolved inline chains with addr2line -i against life_g.so. Its .text is byte-identical to the production build; -g only adds debug info.
Samples: 38.2k (speck_s5, 250 lives), 29.7k (lmax4_s5, 250 lives), 27.7k (speck_s0, 400 lives); about 95 CPU-s in total.
Hottest lines:
- readout kernel.c:174: 7.0%
- the memset inside emit: 5.5%
- hless kernel.c:315: 5.2%
- tick kernel.c:874 (the neighbour occupant's uid check, a cache miss): 3.5%
Calls cost about 18 ns per exp, about 30 ns per log and about 27 ns per tanh.
Files: raw/prof_report_*.txt, raw/prof_*.cc.json, prof_report.py.

findings.claim:
About half the CPU is model arithmetic and half is bookkeeping for exactness, clocklessness and verification.
- Model work (about 50-55%): readout/decode, GRN, membrane, derive, chemistry arithmetic, receptor schedule and thinning.
- Bookkeeping (about 45-50%): heap 15%, hash folding 10%, records + sort + accountant dispatch about 13%, batch dispatch 5%, scheduler, event pool, allocation.
- Hash folding only serves verification: neither the evolution code nor the ledger reads the hashes.
Receptor candidates cost about 25% end to end, including their share of heap, dispatch, records and folds, and more than 95% of them are rejected in SPECK.
findings.evidence:
Cost-centre shares above.
- grep: src/life/evaluate.py, src/run.py and src/evolve.py never read res.hashes.
- Measured with the nohash build: removing fold() alone saves 9.3% CPU, and the ledger stays bitwise identical in 24/24 lives.
- The 25% receptor figure is an estimate: the 54% event share applied to the heap, dispatch and record costs, plus the receptor_next and thinning cost centres, plus 21% of the fold words.

findings.claim: Threads do not contend. The OpenMP region at kernel.c:2206 has nothing shared that is mutable in the hot path: each life callocs its own Ctx, the shared tables are read-only, each life's output row is written once at close, and 'omp critical' guards only the error code. Allocation is negligible. Peak memory is under 1 MB per life.
findings.evidence:
Code reading:
- run_one: calloc(Ctx), ctx_free at the end.
- close_life writes the 57 ledger doubles and run_one copies the 5 hashes, once per life.
- '#pragma omp critical' covers only rc = r on failure.
- schedule(dynamic,1) costs one atomic per 0.1-s life.
Measured:
- Batch process CPU at threads=2 vs 1: 4.52 vs 4.58 s, 2.41 vs 2.46 s, 3.81 vs 3.77 s. Weak test: under load the two threads overlapped only partly (CPU/wall 0.5-1.2).
- Hashes are identical for per-life calls and batch calls at threads 1 and 2.
- grow() runs 158-258 reallocs per life; libc time is 0.2-0.3% of samples.
- Peak capacity of all life arrays: 0.74-0.97 MB at T=1024.
- Process maxrss is 198-225 MB, almost all of it Python, numpy and torch.

findings.claim:
Build flags (24 lives each, paired life by life against prod):
- -march=x86-64-v2/v3/native with -ffp-contract=off is bitwise identical (hashes and ledger 24/24) and only 1.2%, 2.8% and 3.1% faster.
- FMA contraction (-ffp-contract=fast) changes every hash (0/24) for a 1.5% gain. It would also break the bitwise match with reference.py, which rounds every operation.
- -O2 is 3.4% slower.
v3 also matched on 192 random-genome lives.
findings.evidence:
variants.py: each life ran once per variant, the variants interleaved so that load drift cancels; numbers are geometric means of the CPU ratio.
Ratios: v2 0.988, v3 0.972, native 0.969, O2 1.034, fma 0.985, nohash 0.907.
v2 removes the libm calls to nearbyint (nm -D); with v3, floor is still imported.
broad_check.py: v3 hashes 192/192.
Files: raw/analyse_variants.txt, raw/broad_check.json.

findings.claim:
Prototype speedups I built and measured (scratch copies only):
- 'fast' mode (no hash folds, no R_PACKET records: the simulator counts packets and pushes flights itself): 20.8% less CPU (1.26x), ledger bitwise identical everywhere tested.
- 'ro' (readout and GRN sums skip the +0.0 weights of inactive genes, 4 knobs interleaved, a zero result recomputed in full): 2.2% faster, hashes identical.
- fast + ro + x86-64-v3: 25.8-26.7% less CPU (1.35-1.36x), ledger bitwise identical.
- Floyd bottom-up heap pop: no gain (+1%).
findings.evidence:
opt_patch.py; raw/analyse_variants_opt.txt and raw/analyse_variants_bu.txt.
CPU ratios: ro 0.978, fast 0.792, fastro 0.773, fastro_v3 0.733 / 0.742 (two runs), bu 1.010, fastro_bu_v3 0.738.
Ledger checks for fast/fastro/fastro_v3:
- the 3 bodies: 24/24
- 192 random-genome lives at T=160 (74 guard trips, 80 bodies over 50 cells): 192/192
- 36 lives with kill_frac 0.4 at t=200 (907 kills, lost packets, nonzero in-flight morphogen): 36/36
The ro and bu builds kept hashes identical everywhere tested, which also confirms that the pop order among equal heap keys does not matter.

findings.claim:
Bitwise reproducibility across machines is not guaranteed.
- build.py pins only gcc flags (no compiler, glibc or CPU check), and LIFE_ABI.md section 2 assumes the same libm.
- glibc 2.39 chooses exp/log/pow/sin/cos/tanh code at runtime by CPU feature. Its FMA and non-FMA paths disagree on 5e-6 to 1e-3 of inputs (up to 1 ULP, 3 ULP for tanh).
- With the non-FMA path, every life's hashes change (0/24 equal). The ledger stayed identical in 21/24 lives; the others differed only in dist_sum, X_end and path, and F was identical in all 24.
- Discrete events are robust because of the q10/q8 quantisation, but over 1000 lives x 500 generations a decision will flip eventually, so evolution would diverge.
findings.evidence:
libm_fp.c over 2e6 inputs: fingerprint 0debfc91371c03c8 by default, bb8e3d1fc4edfa8a with GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.cpu.hwcaps=-AVX2,-FMA,-FMA4,-AVX. ld.so --list-diagnostics confirmed that the FMA/AVX/AVX2 bits were cleared.
Per-input differences out of 200k: exp 133-145, log 24, pow 138-198, tanh 26, sin 156, cos 132 (raw/libm_variant_diff.txt).
Lives (raw/variants_nofma.jsonl): H_ALL and H_CHEM differ in every life, H_WORLD in 9/24.
Any modern x86 server (Intel Haswell or later, AMD Zen) has FMA and AVX2, so it takes the same path. A different glibc version, ARM, or a CPU without AVX2 is the risk.

findings.claim: The repo already has a working tripwire for a new machine. The golden-hash tests pass here and fail under the emulated non-FMA libm. The section 14 test vectors exercise each libm function at only one or two points, so they would miss this. My xmachine_check.py with xmachine_ref.json compares the libm fingerprint plus 24 evolved-body lives (all 5 hashes and all 57 ledger columns): BITWISE OK here, MISMATCH under the non-FMA emulation.
findings.evidence:
pytest -p no:cacheprovider on test_life_world_bell.py::test_bell_lives_are_bitwise_those_of_the_abi2_kernel and test_life_world_catch.py::test_bodies_without_holes_live_bitwise_as_before_the_filled_footprint, with CELL_DEV_CACHE set to my scratch dir: 2 passed.
Under GLIBC_TUNABLES non-FMA both fail, on 'BUSY hex' and 'ring 2 + 2 hidden L4'.
The .so built from the repo has the same .text as lib/life_prod.so.
raw/xmachine_nofma.txt: hashes 0/8 per body, ledger 7/8, 8/8 and 6/8.

findings.claim: Outside the kernel, evolution's mutation noise depends on the CPU too. torch.randn with the same seed gives different numbers under ATEN_CPU_CAPABILITY=avx2 and =default. A rented AVX-512 machine would pick other kernels unless ATEN_CPU_CAPABILITY=avx2 is set and torch stays at 2.14.1+cpu.
findings.evidence:
src/genome.py:127 and 448 draw mutation noise with torch.randn(generator=gen).
Test: 256x875 randn with seed 123. SHA prefix 4e709a5c... under avx2 vs 42697154... under default.
I could not test AVX-512 on this CPU.

recommendations.change: Add a 'fast' evaluation mode for selection and recheck lives: fold() becomes a no-op, and chemistry packets emit no R_PACKET record (the simulator counts packets[t>=t_open]++ and pushes the flight itself). Use it as a build define or a second exported entry point. Keep the full build for valid, heldout, final and clone lives and for the golden tests. Audit a small sample of selection lives in full mode each generation and require identical ledgers.
recommendations.expected_gain: Measured 20.8% less CPU, 1.26x (paired, 24 lives on 3 bodies). Hashing alone is 9.3%; dropping packet records adds the rest, since they are 58% of all records.
recommendations.preserves_exactness: Ledger stays bitwise identical: 24/24 test lives, 192 random lives, 36 lives with kills. The 5 hashes are not computed (they stay HASH_INIT). Evolution never reads hashes, so evolution results are bitwise unchanged. Heap scheduler only: the window scheduler visits sites out of time order.
recommendations.risk: Two code paths can drift apart, so add a test asserting fast and full ledgers are equal on many random lives. Any future ledger column fed only by R_PACKET records would need the same treatment.

recommendations.change: Build with -march=x86-64-v3 (or v2 for older machines) while keeping -ffp-contract=off and no fast-math. The flags are already part of build.py's cache key. Do not enable FMA contraction.
recommendations.expected_gain: Measured 2.8% (v3) or 1.2% (v2). FMA contraction would add only 1.5% more.
recommendations.preserves_exactness: Bitwise identical, hashes and ledger: 24/24 plus 192/192 lives. The match with reference.py also holds, since every operation is still rounded separately. FMA contraction would change every hash and break the reference match.
recommendations.risk: Requires AVX2/FMA-capable x86 (any server since about 2015). An old CPU would get SIGILL instead of wrong results.

recommendations.change: Make the phenotype readout (a0 + A g, 23x16) and the GRN rows (b + W x, 16x25) sparse and parallel: skip +0.0 weights (inactive gene slots), compute 4 knobs or rows together, and later use AVX2 lanes with A and W transposed (one multiply then one add per lane, same order). If a sum comes out zero, recompute it in full so the sign of zero matches.
recommendations.expected_gain: Measured 2.2% for the scalar prototype ('ro'). Full SIMD is estimated at another 3-5% (the multiply-add work is about 8% of CPU after ro).
recommendations.preserves_exactness: Bitwise identical (hashes 24/24, 192/192, 36/36). Exact by construction: +0.0 times a finite g only flips -0 to +0, and the zero-result fallback handles that case.
recommendations.risk: Low. A future genome that packs -0.0 or a non-finite g would fall back correctly or break the exactness argument, so assert it in a test.

recommendations.change: Replace the binary heap (14-16% of CPU) with a calendar or ladder queue. Use buckets of about 1/32 time unit, since events land 0.5-2.2 units ahead, keep an overflow heap, and keep the exact (t, tie, sk) order.
recommendations.expected_gain: Estimated 5-10%, not measured. Bottom-up pop gave nothing (+1%), so comparison count is not the bottleneck; branchy compares and 24-byte moves are.
recommendations.preserves_exactness: Bitwise identical if the total order is kept. The order among equal keys does not matter: the bu prototype and the window-scheduler contract both show this.
recommendations.risk: Medium: bucket width tuning, and far-future events (kill/stuck, guard) belong in the overflow heap. Validate against the goldens and broad_check.py.

recommendations.change: Cheaper records for the full (hashed) mode. (1) Emit one record per tick carrying all its chemistry packets, and fold the same words in the same order. (2) Stop zeroing all 104 bytes of each Rec; write only the fields each record kind uses.
recommendations.expected_gain: Estimated 4-6% for (1), since records drop from 2.7 to about 1.3 per event, and 2-4% for (2) (the memset alone is 5.5% of samples). Not measured.
recommendations.preserves_exactness: Bitwise identical, hashes included, provided the folded word sequence and the canonical (t, sk, seq) placement are unchanged: a tick's packets are consecutive records of one site at one time.
recommendations.risk: Medium: every reader of a record kind must be checked. Bugs from uninitialised fields can be rare and hard to catch, so run goldens plus broad random-life checks.

recommendations.change: Reject receptor candidates cheaply and exactly. In catch_candidate, compute the acceptance draw first. Reject at once when draw*lam_max >= lam_bg + lam_s*bound, where bound is a rigorous upper bound on the halo from a lower bound on distance (dot displacement bounded by |F|*tau_z/gam). This skips both exps (halo and dot_at) for far cells. Also compute sigma for K_ASYM lazily, at divisions only (about 120 per life against 58k ticks).
recommendations.expected_gain: Estimated 3-5% from the cheap reject (thinning is 5.5-6.7% and more than 95% of SPECK candidates are rejected), plus about 1% from lazy asym. Not measured.
recommendations.preserves_exactness: Bitwise identical only if the bounds are rigorous, including a margin for exp's under-1-ULP error. The lazy asym change is exactly identical.
recommendations.risk: Medium: a too-tight bound silently changes accept decisions. Test on many lives near the halo edge.

recommendations.change: Changes to the model itself (new ABI version and new goldens, best done between experiments). (a) A per-region lambda_max, or candidate streams thinned against a local bound, so most rejected candidates are never created. (b) The kernel's own deterministic exp/log/tanh/pow/sin/cos (only IEEE operations, or vendored correctly rounded CORE-MATH) used by both kernel and reference.py, which also allows vectorised sigma over the 8 active GRN rows.
recommendations.expected_gain: (a) Estimated 15-20%: receptor candidates are about 25% of CPU end to end. (b) A few percent from SIMD sigma, and above all lives become bitwise portable across glibc versions, CPUs and ARM.
recommendations.preserves_exactness: No. (a) keeps the statistics but changes every life. (b) changes every result by about 1 ULP-level divergence against current goldens, then is exactly reproducible everywhere.
recommendations.risk: Re-validation against all gates and goldens. The Python reference gets slower if it must run a pure-Python exp.

recommendations.change: Parallelise across runs before parallelising within one. Lives are independent and threads do not contend, so on a many-core machine run many independent runs (seeds and controls) at 2-4 threads each instead of one run with many threads. Within a call, order lives longest first (for example by parent body size, or the parent's events last generation) to shorten the barrier tail. Each generation has two barriers: the 768-life selection call, then the 256-life recheck call.
recommendations.expected_gain: Throughput scales about with core count. LPT order mostly matters when a call has 8 or fewer lives per thread (the recheck at 32+ threads): estimated 5-20% of that call's wall time. Measure with idle_scaling.py order/layout.
recommendations.preserves_exactness: Yes. Results do not depend on thread count, batch composition or order (hashes were identical for per-life and batch calls at threads 1 and 2), and the evaluator averages each genome's lives in a fixed order.
recommendations.risk: Low. If the life order is permuted inside build.run, it must be un-permuted before the outputs are averaged.

recommendations.change:
Before trusting results on rented compute:
- Use an image matching this laptop: Ubuntu 24.04 (glibc 2.39), gcc 13.3, torch 2.14.1+cpu, the same numpy.
- Choose x86-64 with AVX2 and FMA (AMD EPYC Zen 3/4 or Intel Ice Lake or later).
- Set ATEN_CPU_CAPABILITY=avx2.
- Run xmachine_check.py xmachine_ref.json and the two golden tests, and require BITWISE OK.
CPU instances only: a GPU does not help an exact, branchy, event-driven kernel. Each job needs about 0.3 GB and each life under 1 MB, so pick compute-optimised instances on core count and per-core speed.
recommendations.expected_gain: Not a speedup. It keeps rented runs comparable with the 29-run pilot and checkable against it bit for bit.
recommendations.preserves_exactness: It is what makes exactness hold across machines. Without it, hashes differ, ledgers differ in about 12% of lives in low-order bits, and evolution diverges eventually.
recommendations.risk: An AVX-512 host still runs the kernel bitwise alike, since glibc picks the same FMA path, but torch would use other kernels unless pinned. ARM (Graviton) would almost certainly differ.

verdict.title: Review of the 'kernel' efficiency report: the main numbers hold up. Fast mode measures 1.24x (the report says 1.26x), the whole run gains about 1.23x, and the report misses founder cost, the slowest-run limit, and a hash-equality hazard in fast mode

checks.claim: One life of an evolved CATCH body costs 0.07-0.15 CPU-s at T=1024 on one E-core, which is 1.2-1.5 us per cell-time unit.
checks.recheck: I compiled my own prod build from src/life/kernel.c with build.py's flags; it came out byte-identical to the report's lib/life_prod.so. I loaded it with my own ctypes wrapper (verify/vload.py) and timed thread CPU around life_run, threads=1, nice 19, pinned to E-cores 4-11. I used new seeds (first=7100-7400), T cycling over 768/1024/1536, and 10 pilot bodies (verify/check.py, raw/check_{a,b,c}.jsonl).
checks.result:
CPU-s per life scaled to T=1024:
- speck_s5: 0.150 s (report 0.150)
- speck_s0: 0.078 s (report 0.074)
- lmax4_s5: 0.130 s (report 0.118)

Us per cell-unit: 1.34, 1.29 and 1.59. The other 7 bodies came out at 1.32-1.52 (one tiny body excluded).

Load bias, measured: the E-cores ran at 2.5-2.8 GHz against a 4.3 GHz maximum. A P-core whose SMT sibling was busy gave the same per-life CPU as an E-core (0.150 vs 0.146 s). An LP core was 1.9x slower (0.275 s, 1.44 GHz). So these absolute numbers are tied to the clock, and an idle or server core should be noticeably faster.

checks.claim: The heap processes about 2x as many events as the ledger 'events' column counts. Receptor candidates are 43-60% of heap pops, about 4% of them are accepted in SPECK (20% in v1), and R_PACKET is about 58% of records.
checks.recheck: I wrote my own counting patch (verify/vcount_patch.py → kernel_vc.c), with thread-local counters on hpop by event group/sub, on hpush, and on emit by record kind. I ran 6 new-seed lives per body (verify/vcount.py). Acceptance also comes from the ledger columns rec_accept/rec_cand of all 62 checked lives.
checks.result:
Heap pops vs ledger events:

verdict.corrected_recommendations:
Ranked by value per effort. Gains are measured on this loaded laptop unless marked as estimates.

1. **Rent a many-core x86 CPU machine and run many runs side by side.**
   - Exact, no code changes. This is by far the biggest lever.
   - Lives are independent, the threads do not contend (from reading the code), and results do not depend on thread count or order (verified). Per-life memory is under 1 MB, and each job needs about 0.3 GB.
   - A whole 29-run pilot, about 217 thread-hours on the laptop, finishes in roughly the slowest run's time. Neither the report nor I have measured how fast a server core is relative to the laptop's, so run the report's idle_bench.sh and xmachine_check.py on the rented host first.
   - A GPU would not help.

2. **Give the slowest runs more threads.** Exact; small effort. The report missed this.
   - The makespan is set by the big-body runs: speck_s6 took 9.7 h and speck_s7 9.2 h, at 3 threads each.
   - From the measured parts of a generation plus the simulated barriers, one run should scale to about 5.1x at 16 threads (ideal 5.3), about 9.9x at 32 and about 18x at 64, all relative to 3 threads. At 64 threads the 0.3% serial Python share grows to about 5%.
   - Let each run choose its thread count every generation, for example in proportion to pop_body, or from the cores left free when small runs finish. This is exact because results do not depend on thread count.
   - "Parallelise across runs before within one" is right for throughput, but up to about 16-32 threads per run is cheap.

3. **'fast' kernel mode for selection, recheck and founder lives.**
   - Measured at 0.806 CPU, i.e. 1.24x, 95% CI 1.22-1.26x, over 62 lives on 10 bodies plus kills and noise. The report's 1.26x came from 3 bodies. The ledger was bitwise identical in 62/62 lives.
   - For a whole run, after Amdahl: about 1.23x if the every-10 rounds stay in full mode, since founders can use it too.
   - Effort is small: a #define or a second entry point, opt-in per call.
   - Required safeguards: build.load() must keep returning the full build. scripts/life_gates.py and the tests compare hashes, and with fast mode all hashes are HASH_INIT, so those comparisons would always pass. Add a test that fast and full ledgers are equal on random lives, plus a per-generation audit.

4. **Add -march=x86-64-v3 and the sparse 'ro' readout on top of fast.**
   - fastro_v3 measured 0.741, i.e. 1.35x, ledger 62/62. v3 alone is 2.0%, not 2.8%, but it combines with ro: fastro_v3 / (fast x v3) = 0.94.
   - Small effort, exact. Hashes for v3 were 62/62 identical.
   - Requires AVX2+FMA hosts; an older CPU gets SIGILL rather than wrong results.

5. **Run the every-10 measurement rounds off the critical path.** Exact; small to medium effort; missed by the report.
   - The valid, held-out and clone lives only feed the logs, not selection, so another worker can run them while the next generation starts. That saves about 4% of wall per run, a bit more at high thread counts.

6. **Pin the platform for reproducibility.** Small effort.
   - Use an Ubuntu 24.04 / glibc 2.39 container with the same venv (torch 2.14.1+cpu), and set ATEN_CPU_CAPABILITY=avx2.
   - Use x86 hosts with AVX2+FMA.
   - Run xmachine_check.py and the two golden tests first.
   - This buys bit-for-bit replay and passing golden tests, not scientific validity. In 18 lives under non-FMA libm, F was identical in all of them and the ledger in 17. Treat ARM as untested rather than as known to differ.

7. **LPT (longest-first) ordering of lives within a call.** Exact, but low value: under 1% of a generation at 16 or fewer threads per run, about 2-4% at 64. Only worth doing for runs with very many threads.

8. **Unmeasured exact kernel changes, each medium effort and estimated at 3-10%:**
   - calendar queue in place of the binary heap
   - one record per tick, and no full memset of each record
   - cheap exact rejection of receptor candidates

   Prototype them only if the compute bill becomes large, and validate against the goldens and broad random-life checks.

9. **Changes to the model itself** (per-region lambda_max, the kernel's own libm). Large effort. They change every life, so do them between experiments.
verdict.missed:
**Costs the report leaves out**
- **Founder phase.** It takes 530-1130 s per run: 5.8% of the pilot's total wall time, and 50-70% of the wall time of the 13 small-body runs. It is embarrassingly parallel (32,768 lives) and can use fast mode, but the report's planning ignores it.
- **The slowest run sets the pilot's length.** The longest run takes 9.7 h at 3 threads, so renting many cores alone does not shorten a pilot unless the heavy runs also get more threads. Results do not depend on thread count, so changing it per generation is safe.

**Measurement biases**
- **Clock and core type.** During the measurements the E-cores ran at 2.5-2.8 GHz against a 4.3 GHz maximum. A P-core thread whose SMT sibling was busy ran no faster than an E-core. The LP cores (12-13) are 1.9x slower per life, so a pilot thread landing on them becomes a straggler; on the laptop, keep runs off cpus 12-13.
- **SMT on rented machines.** Cloud vCPUs are usually hyperthreads. For this branchy, latency-bound kernel, compare cost per physical core, or pick instances where one vCPU is one core. I believe AWS's 7th-generation AMD instances work that way; confirm on the provider's page.
- **Straggler workload.** idle_scaling.py builds its workload from parent lives only, so it understates the cost variance of a real generation (mutants, guard trips) and with it any LPT benefit.

**A hazard in fast mode**
- In fast mode every hash stays HASH_INIT. Any code that treats "hashes equal" as "lives identical" would silently pass: scripts/life_gates.py and the golden tests do this. Fast mode has to stay an explicit opt-in.

**Design-level levers (not exact)**
- The two-stage recheck is 23.6% of generation wall time. A smaller recheck_k or recheck_lives would save time but changes the experiment.
- So does drawing T from [768, 1024, 1536]: the mean T of 1109 costs about 8% more than the nominal 1024.

**Reproducibility caveats**
- Cross-machine bitwise identity matters for replaying runs and passing golden tests, not for valid statistics. A future OS or glibc upgrade on the laptop itself could also break the goldens; pinning a container protects against both.

**Prices**
- The report gives no prices, so there was nothing to re-check.

report.title: cell-dev evolution loop: where each generation's time goes, how well 4 jobs x 3 threads used the laptop, and what would make rollouts faster on the laptop and on a rented many-core server

findings.claim: Kernel calls in one generation of evolve_life (src/evolve.py about lines 493-600). (A) Population: ev(everyone, draw), 256 genomes x 3 lives = 768 lives in one build.run call (evolve.batch 256). T is drawn per generation from {768, 1024, 1536}. (B) Recheck: the top 64 by mean F on the generation's lives get lives 3-6 of the same draw, 64 x 4 = 256 lives, same T. This call cannot start until A has ranked the population. Every 10 generations (and the last): (C) valid, best x 16 lives at T 1024; (D) held-out, best x 6 worlds x 4 = 24 lives (20 in v1); (E) clone forks, run_forks over the top 8 plus each other breed's best x 3 times x (1 twin + 6 conditions) x 3 lives = 63 full-length lives per genome, 504-880 lives. Founders, once per unseeded run: 16 batches of layout.random(1024) x 2 lives at T 1024, each split into 4 calls of 512 lives, so 64 calls and 32,768 lives. Python between the calls: draw, randint parents, crossover, mutate, origins bookkeeping, ev.table packing (inside t_eval), columns, argsort, pooled(), the curves row, the lineage row (registry, pdist 32x875, json) and file flushes.
findings.evidence: Code read: src/evolve.py (evolve_life, recheck, recheck_draw, sample_founders, fill), src/life/evaluate.py (LifeEvaluator.__call__ splits into chunks of self.batch; run is genome-major), src/life/clones.py run_forks (one build.run for all forks), src/run.py main_life/final_life, scripts/sweep.py (J Popen processes, polled every 2 s), configs/life.yaml + life_catch.yaml + life_speck.yaml. Lives per generation: 1024 kernel lives, plus about 55-90 on average from checkpoints.

findings.claim: Where generation time went in the pilot: the population kernel call took 72.1% of generation wall time, the recheck 23.5%, the checkpoint calls 4.0%, and Python outside the kernel calls 0.2-0.4% (median 13-28 ms per plain generation). Python inside t_eval adds about 30 ms more (packing 256 + 64 genome tables). In total Python costs about 50-75 ms per generation, against 11-32 s mean generation times. Outside the generation loop, founder sampling took 4.4 h of about 78 finished run-hours (~5.6%) and the final evaluation 0.2%. Generations at T 1536 hold 52% of all generation time (T 768: 20%, T 1024: 28%). Generations with more than 5% guard trips hold 0.6%; generations before 20 hold 1.1%.
findings.evidence: loop/pilot_times.py -> pilot_times.txt/json: 28 finished runs, 74.0 generation-hours, from t_gen/t_eval/t_recheck in outputs/catch_pilot/*/curves.jsonl. loop/python_overhead.py -> python_overhead.json (CPU time, nice 19, loaded): breed 14 ms, pack_256 23 ms, pack_64 5.8 ms, build prep 1.6 ms, bookkeeping 1.1 ms. Stuck runs, where kernel work is near zero, give the floor: lmax4 s1 has t_gen 73 ms and t_eval 45 ms for 768 lives. RESULTS.md part 4 also reports recheck 31%/28% of population kernel time; my median recheck/eval ratio over the pilot is 0.32.

findings.claim: Inside one process at 3 threads, almost no thread time is lost: kernel threads were running or runnable 98-99.5% of wall time. At most about 1-2% went to OpenMP barrier tails, Python and I/O together. The rest of the gap is run-queue waiting caused by other load on the machine.
findings.evidence: /proc/<pid>/task/*/schedstat (loop/pilot_threads.py; read-only; earlier snapshot in this session). speck s6, 8.25 h elapsed: each of the 3 kernel threads was on-CPU 88%, waiting in the run queue 10%, and asleep 2%. Workers made about 1,800 voluntary switches, roughly one per kernel call; with libgomp's ~300k-iteration spin, sleep happens only on gaps longer than about 10-20 ms. lmax4 s9: on-CPU 86%, run queue 13.5%. speck s9, 0.38 h: on-CPU 91%, run queue 7.7%, asleep 0.5-1.2%. The simulation below gives 0.3% straggler idle at 3 threads, which fits.

findings.claim: Per-life costs in late generations. Cost follows cell-time: about 1.1 us per cell-unit plus 0.28 us per event (R^2 0.95). The population call's lives spread moderately (cv 0.24-0.98). The longest life in a call is always a mutant that hits the 1024-cell guard: 0.1-0.8% of lives, holding 1-5% of the CPU, but each costing 1.6-1.7 s, or 3-15 times the mean life. Recheck lives are uniform (max/mean 1.4-2.0). The kernel already stops a guard life at the first unit time with n >= n_max (1024) or events > e_max, so the expense is the growth up to 1024 cells.
findings.evidence: 8 replayed generations from 5 finished runs' final populations: speck s5 at T 768/1024/1536, speck s0/s2/s4 at T 1536, lmax4 s5 at T 1024/1536. Children were bred with the run's own crossover+mutate. Totals: 6,144 population, 2,048 recheck and 544 checkpoint lives (loop/gen_replay.py -> replay_*.json; loop/costmodel.py -> costmodel.txt/json). Timing used a copy of kernel.c with per-life thread-CPU clocks (loop/build/kernel_timed.c), checked bitwise equal to the unmodified copy (check_bitwise.py: ledgers and hashes equal). Runs were pinned to E-cores 4-11, 2 threads, nice 19. Absolute times are inflated by load and only relative sizes are used. Guard code: kernel.c guard_check and run_heap; spec.py n_max 1024, e_max 5e6.

findings.claim: Efficiency of one run against its thread count, with schedule(dynamic,1) in kernel order, weighted like the pilot's time over the three T values, checkpoints included, plus ~60 ms of serial Python per generation: 99.6% at 3 threads, 98.8% at 8, 97.6% at 12, 96.4% at 16, 90.8% at 32, 79.5% at 64, 62.9% at 128, 49.9% at 192. The cause is the per-call barrier. From 64 threads up, one guard-tripping life (1.6-1.7 s) is longer than work/P. The small valid and held-out calls (16 and 24 lives) are already 9-12% idle at 3 threads and over 75% idle at 64, but they are under 2% of the work. Batching R runs into each call fixes this: R=4 gives 96.9% at 64 and 79.3% at 192; R=16 gives 99.0% and 94.0%.
findings.evidence: loop/sched_sim.py (exact list-scheduling simulation of OpenMP dynamic,1, from the measured per-life costs) -> sched_sim.txt/json. The same with fitted model costs (sched_sim --model) -> sched_sim_model.txt: same picture. loop/summary.py -> summary.txt/json for the T-weighting and Python. Single-call floors: speck s5 T 768 population with one 1.71 s guard life is 6.4% idle at 16 threads and 40% at 64.

findings.claim: Ordering lives longest-first with a realistic cost guess does not help. A child guessed to cost what its parent costs correlates with its actual cost at only r = -0.04 to 0.30, because life-to-life (seed) variance and mutations dominate. With perfect knowledge of costs (oracle ordering) the gain would be large.
findings.evidence: loop/lpt_pred.py -> lpt_pred.txt/json. Population-call idle, mean of 8 replays: at 64 threads 16.7% in kernel order, 16.2% with the parent-based guess, 4.4% with the oracle; at 192 threads 45.7% / 39.8% / 27.7%.

findings.claim: Founder sampling is dominated by guard trips. 31% of random-genome lives hit the 1024-cell guard (median trip at t 166 of 1024) and hold 82% of founder CPU, so about 4-5% of all pilot compute went to founder lives that cannot become founders. Founder calls of 512 lives are 1.4% idle at 3 threads, 21% at 16 and 62% at 64. Calls of 2,048 lives would be 0.5% / 5.6% / 27% idle, and one call of all 32,768 lives 0.0% / 0.3% / 2.5%.
findings.evidence: loop/founder_sample.py -> founders_speck_lmax4_hexprism_sex_s5_128.json: 128 random genomes x 2 lives at T 1024, speck prior. loop/founder_sim.py -> founder_sim.txt (bootstrap list-scheduling). In the same sample, 4 of 176 non-guard lives peaked at 512 cells or more and 6 at 256 or more. Sample of 256 lives, so the shares are approximate.

findings.claim: How the 4 jobs x 3 threads layout did on the whole sweep. The sweep will span about 24.4 h for 83.2 run-hours. 15% of slot-hours sit idle because the 29th run (speck s9, started about 02:36 today) runs alone on 3 threads for about 5 h. The laptop was also shared: in two 20-30 s samples the pilot got 8.1 and 11.0 of 14 hardware threads (58% and 79%) at load 25-100, with every CPU at 100%. Per-thread speed was low: 1.25-1.9 wall thread-us per cell-unit (median ~1.5) against 0.61 us unloaded in RESULTS.md. My thread-CPU measurements give 1.2-1.5 us, so most of that 2-2.5x slowdown is slower instructions, not time-slicing (run-queue wait is ~10%). Likely causes are the power-limited 15 W U-series chip at all-core load, E-cores sharing L2, hyper-threading and other users' jobs.
findings.evidence: loop/pilot_timeline.py -> pilot_timeline.txt (run start = config.yaml mtime, end = results.jsonl mtime; speck s9's remaining time estimated from the median finished speck run). loop/machine_share.py -> machine_share_1.txt, machine_share_2.txt. loop/pilot_rates.py -> pilot_rates.txt: 3.73e11 population cell-units in 53.4 h of t_eval. lscpu: CPUs 0-3 are 2 P-cores with HT at 5.2 GHz, 4-11 are 8 E-cores at 4.3 GHz in two L2 clusters, 12-13 are 2 LP cores at 2.4 GHz.

findings.claim: On the laptop, the job layout barely matters for throughput: one run is at least 97.6% efficient up to 12 threads, so 4x3, 2x6 and 1x12 differ by under 2%. More threads per run only cut a single run's latency. What does matter is the sweep tail. Simulated on the pilot's own run lengths: the actual order takes 24.4 h; ordering arms by expected length takes 23.6 h; an elastic thread budget (running runs share all 12 threads once fewer than 4 remain) takes 20.8 h, the throughput bound. On a 192-thread server at the pilot's per-thread speed: static 29 slots x 6 threads take 4.9 h with 70% of the box idle; static 16x12 take 2.6 h; elastic takes 1.4-1.5 h. Elastic capped at 32 threads per run takes 1.7 h, and at 16 threads 2.2 h.
findings.evidence: loop/sweep_sim.py -> sweep_sim.txt/json, using pilot_timeline durations and the per-thread-count efficiency curve from summary.py. RESULTS.md (lines ~255-275) also found the machine saturates at ~0.19 R25 generations/s 'whatever the layout'.

findings.claim: Total work, for sizing a rental: the pilot's population calls simulated 3.7e11 cell-units; recheck adds about 32%, checkpoints about 5% and founders about 6%. That is about 83 run-hours x 3 threads, roughly 250 loaded-laptop thread-hours or about 220 CPU-hours. The longest single run is about 9.7 h at 3 loaded threads, about 29 thread-hours. On any machine, a sweep's floor is max(total work / threads, longest run / efficiency at the threads it gets).

recommendations.change: Elastic thread budget. sweep.py gets a total thread count, rewrites a per-run budget file (for example floor(total / running runs), at least 1) whenever runs start or finish, and LifeEvaluator.run (and the build.run calls in clones and final_life) re-reads its thread count before each kernel call instead of fixing cfg.threads at start.
recommendations.expected_gain: Laptop sweep 24.4 h -> 20.8 h (-15%); this pilot's 5 h single-run tail would shrink to about 1.5 h. On a 192-thread server it is the largest lever: 4.9 h (static 29x6) -> ~1.5 h at the same per-thread speed, about 3.3x fewer rented hours.
recommendations.preserves_exactness: Yes, bitwise. Results do not depend on the thread count (documented in LifeEvaluator; the benchmark's bitwise check confirms 1 vs 2 threads). Only timing fields change.
recommendations.risk: Low. Keep the budget at least 1 and avoid brief oversubscription when a new run starts; the change touches only how threads are handed out.

recommendations.change: Rented many-core server: run many runs at once, at most 16-32 threads each while many are active, and let survivors widen as others finish (elastic). Do not give a single run more than about 32 threads unless lives are batched across runs. Use x86 compute-optimized many-core CPUs; there is no GPU use. Memory is about 0.3-0.45 GB per process.
recommendations.expected_gain: One run's efficiency is 96% at 16 threads and 91% at 32, against 80% at 64 and 50% at 192. A pilot-sized sweep (29 x 500 generations) would need about 1.4-1.5 h on 192 threads if a vCPU is as fast as a loaded laptop thread; it is probably faster (unloaded laptop threads are 2-2.5x faster than loaded ones).
recommendations.preserves_exactness: Yes. It changes only layout and threads.
recommendations.risk: Per-vCPU speed on the server is unmeasured. Run bench_scaling.py kernel/layouts on a short rental first; with SMT, count a vCPU as roughly 0.6 of a core.

recommendations.change: Founder sampling: (a) config evolve.batch=1024 or more (genomes per kernel call); (b) small code change: under founder_all, draw all 16 batches first (same layout.random and draw-index order) and run their 32,768 lives in one kernel call.
recommendations.expected_gain: Founder-call idle at 16 threads 21% -> 5.6% with (a), 0.3% with (b); at 64 threads 62% -> 27% / 2.5%. On the laptop at 3 threads only 1.4% -> ~0% of founder time (~0.1% overall). It matters when founders run wide on a server: founders are ~6% of run-hours and come first in every run.
recommendations.preserves_exactness: Yes, bitwise. evolve.batch only chunks the genomes (LifeEvaluator.__call__ concatenates per-genome results), and (b) keeps the same RNG call order and founder seeds.
recommendations.risk: Low. Check that collect/life_census still get per-batch results.

recommendations.change: Batch several runs per kernel call: R runs advance in lockstep inside one process; their population calls are joined into one kernel call, then their rechecks.
recommendations.expected_gain: One-run efficiency at 64 / 192 threads goes 80% / 50% -> 97% / 79% with R=4, and 99% / 94% with R=16. Worth it only if few runs must go very wide (for example one long run on a big box); with elastic multi-process layouts the gain is small.
recommendations.preserves_exactness: Yes. Lives are independent and each run keeps its own RNG, seeds and files.
recommendations.risk: Medium: a rewrite of the evolve_life driver and lineage I/O, and runs of very different lengths drift apart.

recommendations.change: Take the diagnostics off the critical path: clones.every 20 instead of 10, or fold the valid, held-out and fork lives of generation g into generation g+1's population call (they never feed selection).
recommendations.expected_gain: clones.every 20 saves about 2% of wall time (checkpoints are 4.0%). Folding saves the small calls' barrier idle: under 0.5% at 16 threads or fewer, 3-4 points at 128-192.
recommendations.preserves_exactness: The evolution stays bitwise identical either way. clones.every changes only which generations get diagnostic rows (not comparable with the pilot's every-10 clone curves); folding is exact but delays the rows by one generation.
recommendations.risk: Low.

recommendations.change: Laptop hygiene for sweeps: keep other heavy jobs off (the pilot got only 58-79% of hardware threads at load 25-100), and do not count on more threads per run raising throughput.
recommendations.expected_gain: Up to 1.3-1.7x the machine share for the sweep. Faster per-thread speed would follow too (the unloaded laptop measured 0.61 us per cell-unit against ~1.5 us loaded).
recommendations.preserves_exactness: Yes.
recommendations.risk: None in code; it limits other uses of the laptop.

recommendations.change: Optional, the user's call: the pilot's last run (speck s9, started ~02:36) is alone on 3 threads for ~5 h. It could be restarted with threads=12, which gives identical results (thread count does not affect them).
recommendations.expected_gain: About 3-3.5 h sooner end of the pilot.
recommendations.preserves_exactness: Yes, bitwise (thread-independent), but the restart repeats the ~0.4 h already done.
recommendations.risk: sweep.py would log the killed run as failed and the aggregate step would need a manual rerun; it also competes with the other analysis on the machine. I did not touch the process.

recommendations.change: Not recommended: (1) asynchronous / steady-state evolution with no generation barrier; (2) merging the population and recheck calls; (3) longest-first ordering with the current cost guesses; (4) a lower n_max for selection lives.
recommendations.expected_gain: (1) The barrier costs only 1-9% at 32 threads or fewer per run. (2) Exact merging is impossible because the recheck needs the population's ranking; rechecking everyone costs +75% lives. (3) No measurable gain (64-thread idle 16.7% -> 16.2%). (4) Would cut the guard stragglers, but bodies already reach 300-400 cells (s0 population q90 305, still growing).
recommendations.preserves_exactness: (1) and (4) change the algorithm and break comparability with the pilot; (2) as speculative recheck-all changes the work but could stay exact; (3) is exact but useless.
recommendations.risk: High for (1) and (4): different evolutionary dynamics.

recommendations.change: Founder-only guard (for example n_max 512 during founder sampling only).
recommendations.expected_gain: Up to ~3-5x less founder CPU (82% of it is guard lives), i.e. ~4% of total run time; much more for runs that stay stuck at 1-2 cells, where founders are about half of the run.
recommendations.preserves_exactness: No. Founder selection changes if a top-8 founder would have peaked above the cap (in my sample 4 of 176 non-guard lives peaked at 512 cells or more).
recommendations.risk: Medium. Adopt only after checking on the pilot seeds that the chosen founders are bitwise unchanged.

checks.claim: Where generation time goes: the population kernel call takes 72.1%, the recheck 23.5%, checkpoints 4.0% and Python 0.2-0.4%. Founders are 5.6% of run-hours and the final evaluation 0.2%. Generations at T 768/1024/1536 hold 20/28/52% of generation time.
checks.recheck: I wrote my own accounting (verify/v_timeline.py) over the curves.jsonl and results.jsonl of the 28 finished runs. Founder time is wall_s minus the sum of t_gen. Checkpoint generations are g%10==0 or the final one. I also read evolve.py to see what t_gen covers.
checks.result: Population 72.1%, recheck 23.6%, checkpoint extra 4.1%, Python residual 0.24%. Founders 4.41 h of 78.2 h (5.6%), final 0.17 h (0.22%). By T: 19.9 / 28.1 / 52.0%. Median recheck/eval ratio 0.31. One nuance: t_gen is stopped before the lineage write, so founder time also includes setup and every generation's lineage I/O. Both are small.

checks.claim: One run's efficiency against its thread count, with schedule(dynamic,1), T-weighted, with 60 ms of serial Python: 99.6% at 3 threads, 98.8% at 8, 97.6% at 12, 96.4% at 16, 90.8% at 32, 79.5% at 64, 62.9% at 128, 49.9% at 192. The cause is a 1.6-1.7 s guard-tripping life, and the longest life in a call is always a guard mutant.
checks.recheck: Own heap-based list scheduler (verify/v_sched.py) on the 8 replays' per-life thread-CPU costs, population plus recheck, same T weights. I also checked n_peak and status of the longest life in each population call.
checks.result: The efficiencies reproduce: 99.6 / 98.8 / 97.7 / 96.5 / 90.9 / 79.8 / 63.2 / 50.2%. The mechanism is overstated. The longest life is not a guard trip in 3 of 8 replays (n_peak 219, 394 and 532). Only 3 of 8 replays have a 1.6-1.7 s life. In s0 and s2 the guard lives cost 0.4-1.0 s. The recheck call has no guard lives at all and is still 40-46% idle at 192 threads and 18-19% at 64. So at high thread counts the loss comes as much from having too few lives per call (256 or 768) as from guard stragglers.

verdict.corrected_recommendations:
Ranked by value per effort. "Loaded-laptop speed" means pilot per-thread speed. My test lives were bitwise identical at 1 and 2 threads, so these layout changes do not change results.

1. Change the job layout, no code needed: run fewer runs at once, each with more threads.
   - Laptop: sweep.py --jobs 1 --threads 12, or --jobs 2 --threads 6. For this pilot's mix of run lengths, that gives about 21.2-21.9 h instead of 24.5 h.
   - 192-core server: --jobs 6-8 --threads 24-32 gives 1.4-1.8 h at loaded-laptop speed. Do not use 29x6 (4.9 h) or 16x12 (2.5 h).
   - Start the expected-long arms (speck) first; that alone moves 8x24 from 1.76 h to 1.40 h.
   - Gain: about 13% on the laptop and 3x on the server against the naive layout. Almost everything the report credited to elastic threads.

2. Rent one c7a.48xlarge, or another no-SMT many-core AMD machine.
   - It has 192 physical cores and costs $9.85/h on demand or $3.40/h spot.
   - A pilot-sized sweep (29 runs x 500 generations) is about 220-250 loaded-laptop CPU-hours. If a server core is 1-2x a loaded laptop thread (unmeasured), that is about 0.8-1.5 h, roughly $8-15 on demand, against about 25 h on the laptop.
   - Before the sweep, spend about 15 minutes on two checks:
     - bench_scaling.py kernel and layouts, to measure per-core speed;
     - a bitwise check of a fixed set of lives against laptop hashes, because exactness assumes the same libm. Use the same Ubuntu 24.04 / glibc 2.39 / gcc 13.3 image.
   - Use on-demand: there is no resume support, so a spot interruption would lose runs.
   - Effort: small. Value: very high.

3. Elastic thread budget (small code change, bitwise exact).
   - Over the best static layout it adds 0-23% when run lengths are unknown in advance. On the laptop: 20.8 h against 21.2 h for 1x12.
   - Mainly robustness against an unpredictable long tail.
   - On a laptop shared with the user's own analyses, it moves CPU from those jobs to the pilot rather than adding capacity.

4. Founders: set evolve.batch=1024 (config only, exact). It saves about 1% of a sweep where runs use 16-32 threads, and about nothing on the laptop. One kernel call for all 16 founder batches (small code, needs a separate draw per batch) adds about another 1%.

5. Laptop hygiene: keep other heavy jobs off during sweeps. The pilot's share of the machine would go from 58-79% to about 100%, so up to 1.3-1.7x. The per-thread gain is at most about 1.4x (0.97 us at 8 threads unloaded), not the 2.5x the report implied.

6. clones.every 20: about 2%. It changes when diagnostic rows appear, so they are not comparable with the pilot's every-10 clone curves.

7. Batching several runs into each kernel call: large effort and little value for sweeps, because wide static layouts already reach 1.40 h against a 1.30 h work bound. Only useful for a single run spread over 64 or more threads.

8. Restarting speck s9 with 12 threads: the user's call. It saves about 3 h of pilot tail, repeats about 0.75 h of done work, and takes CPU from the user's running analysis.

Keep as not recommended:
- asynchronous evolution;
- longest-first ordering with parent-based guesses;
- a lower n_max;
- a founder-only guard, unless it is shown not to change the chosen founders.
verdict.missed:
1. The zero-code fix: wider, fewer jobs (laptop 1x12 or 2x6; server 6-8 x 24-32, longest arms first) captures nearly all the gain the report credits to elastic threads. The 3.3x server figure compares elastic against a naive 29x6 layout.

2. Dollars, which answer the rental question directly. A pilot-sized sweep is about $8-15 on demand on a c7a.48xlarge ($9.85/h; $3.40/h spot), against about 25 h on the laptop. c7i-class machines with SMT cost about 1.7x more per physical core for this CPU-bound, no-GPU work. Cost scales with total work, so a 64-core box costs about the same and just takes 3x longer.

3. Exactness across machines. docs/LIFE_ABI.md says bitwise agreement assumes the same libm (exp, log, tanh, cos, sin, pow). The report marked renting as "exact: yes" without checking. Pin the OS image and compare hashes on a fixed set of lives before trusting results as comparable with the pilot.

4. No resume or checkpoint support exists (nothing in run.py, evolve.py or sweep.py), so spot instances risk losing whole runs. Use on-demand, or add resume (population, ids, origins, generator state, counters) only if sweeps grow much larger.

5. At 64 or more threads per run, idle comes from having too few lives per call (recheck 256, population 768), not only from guard stragglers. The recheck call has no guard lives and is still 40-46% idle at 192 threads.

6. The report's 15% idle and 24.4 h depend on an unknown s9 length (3-9 h gives a 22.4-28.4 h span).

7. The laptop's tail threads are not idle: load 25-30 from the user's other analysis at nice 19 is using them.

8. The schedstat on-CPU share includes libgomp spin-waiting, so it does not by itself show useful work.

9. The founder guard share is 27.7% across all runs' full censuses, not 31%.

10. Future cost growth. Per-life cost follows cell-time, and bodies are still growing (s0 population q90 about 305 cells against about 120 for s5). Later or longer runs will cost about 2-3x more per generation than the pilot average, so budget rentals on cell-time rather than run count.

11. On a two-socket, many-CCD server, pinning each job's threads to one NUMA node or CCD set (taskset, OMP_PROC_BIND) is a cheap, exact extra. It is unmeasured.

report.title: Sample efficiency of cell-dev selection: late-run rollouts mostly rank near-neutral children by capture-count noise

findings.claim: Where the pilot's compute goes. Selection lives take 69% of process time, the recheck 22%, monitoring (valid, held-out and clone forks, plus breeding and logging overhead) 4%, founder sampling 4.6% and the final evaluation 0.2%. 95% of generation time falls in generations whose median body has at least 30 cells.
findings.evidence: lineage_stats.py over all 29 runs (curves.jsonl t_eval / t_recheck / t_gen; founders = results wall_s - sum(t_gen) - final_s). Process-hours: eval 49.4, recheck 16.0, rest 2.9, founders 3.3, final 0.1, total 71.7. A 500-generation run uses 384k selection lives, 128k recheck lives, 0.8k valid, 1.0-1.2k held-out, about 26k clone or fork lives (8 genomes x 3 times x 7 x 3 every 10 generations) and 32.8k founder lives. Generations with median_n >= 30 account for 65.4 of 68.8 generation-hours (5953 of 12546 generations). Load bias: these are wall-clock times under 4 jobs x 3 threads plus other load. All phases run in the same process under the same load, so the split is roughly fair, but absolute hours are inflated.

findings.claim: Among the top genomes, selection is close to a lottery. Each generation 27-28 of the 32 survivors are new children and only 4-6 parents survive. Parents fill 8-10 of the 64 shortlist slots. If parents and children were exchangeable (no true differences), the expected numbers would be 4 kept and 8 in the shortlist. Inside the shortlist, the Spearman correlation between F_base (3 lives) and F_recheck (4 lives) has a median of 0.034 over 8,514 body-run generations, and 0.000-0.017 in generations >= 450.
findings.evidence: lineage.jsonl from the 20 runs whose median body reached 30 cells: per-run medians are kept 26-28, parents kept 4-6, parents in shortlist 8-10, recheck_changed 7.5-12. Repeated measures of genomes shortlisted in several generations (F_recheck centred per generation, never the value they were shortlisted on) give a between-genome ICC of 0.00-0.065 in every body run. File: samples/lineage_stats.json.

findings.claim: The near-zero recheck correlation is both range restriction and genuine noise, and the experiment reproduces the logs. All real between-genome variance comes from about 4-9% broken children, which never reach the top 64. Among parents and the remaining near-neutral children, true spread is at most 0.27 F (speck) or 0.135 F (catch_v1), against a per-life noise sd of 2.0 F (speck) or 0.62 F (catch_v1).
findings.evidence: crn_experiment.py: the final population (32) plus 224 children bred exactly as evolve_life does (crossover then mutate, same n_mut, p_cell and scaling), 16 shared fresh lives at T 1024. speck s5 (about 120 cells): per-life genome x life variance 4.05 (sd 2.01); shared life effect 0.47; between-genome variance 1.47 over all 256, but 0.046 among parents (95% upper bound 0.25) and 0.025 among the 237 non-broken genomes (tau about 0.16, 95% upper bound 0.27). Broken children are 8.5% (mean F 2.78 vs parents 6.49). Emulating the pilot's recheck on these numbers gives Spearman 0.001 (10-90%: -0.16 to 0.16), 9.7 parents in the shortlist, 5.4 parents kept, winner's curse 1.42 F and a variance of 0.97 for the 4-life recheck means; the logs at gens >= 450 show 0.009, 10, 5, 1.31 and 1.21. catch_v1 lmax4 s5 (about 75 cells): noise sd 0.62, life effect 0.155, cloud tau 0.11 (upper bound 0.135), 4.5% broken; emulated Spearman 0.013 against 0.017 in the logs. Single-life heritability is 0.27 (speck) and 0.14 (catch) over all candidates but 0.006 and 0.030 inside the near-neutral cloud. Files: samples/runs/*/noise.json and noise_L16.txt.

findings.claim: Per-life F noise in SPECK is Poisson noise in the capture count. Each capture is worth R_cap/T = 0.49 F, and a 120-cell body makes about 19 captures per T=1024 life. Neither the seed scheme nor any other bookkeeping can remove it: only observing more captures (more simulated time) does.
findings.evidence: speck s5, 256 genomes x 16 lives: per-genome per-life variance of F has median 4.39, against the Poisson prediction (R_cap/T)^2 x mean captures = 4.50 (ratio 0.99). The index of dispersion of captures within a genome is 0.98, and the within-genome correlation of F with captures is 0.99. catch_v1 (R_cap 100) makes about 55 captures per life, which predicts a per-life sd of 0.68 (measured 0.62).

findings.claim: Common random numbers are already in place, but they help little late in a run, because the clockless dynamics decorrelate after any genome change. Early in a run they are decisive. Every genome of a generation and its recheck shares the life seeds (hash of run seed, purpose, generation and life) and the per-generation T. Late in the run CRN is worth only 1.1-1.6x in lives.
findings.evidence: Paired-difference variance per life, different seeds divided by same seeds: speck s5 1.13-1.15 for children vs parent a (per-life correlation 0.13) and 0.93-0.96 for point mutants vs the best (no gain). catch_v1 s5: 1.54-1.60 for children (correlation 0.35) and 1.56-1.81 for mutants. Small-body population (lmax4 s0, 2 cells): 7.2-13x, child correlation 0.92, mutant correlation 0.9999, and 11% of mutants are bitwise neutral. In the scheme simulator, the pilot without CRN loses 1% of its selection differential in speck, 9% in catch and 22% in the 2-cell regime (86% to 67% of the oracle). Source: evaluate.py life_seed / LifeDraw and evolve.recheck_draw.

findings.claim: Effect sizes are bimodal. A few children and mutants are clearly broken, and one life detects them. All others differ by less than the resolution of any feasible number of lives. Ranking a typical near-neutral mutant against its parent with 80% probability takes about 70-200 lives in SPECK and 25-80 in catch_v1. The pilot gives a child 3 lives and the shortlist 7.
findings.evidence: speck s5: of 64 point mutants of the best, 4.7% have z < -3 (median 0.4 lives for an 80% call) and none have z > 3. Of 224 children vs parent a, 5.4% have z < -3 and 0.4% have z > 3. Paired per-life sd is 2.76 F. Using n80 = (0.84 x sd_d / delta)^2: delta 0.27 (upper bound) needs 74 lives, 0.16 (point estimate) 211, 0.5 needs 22, 1.0 needs 5. catch_v1: paired sd about 0.8, cloud tau 0.11, so 37 lives at delta = tau and 83 at the median |delta|. 2-cell regime: with CRN the paired sd is 0.0015, so a typical mutant is resolved in under 1 life. Mutational load in speck: children average 0.47 F below their parents (0.31 of it from broken children); catch: 0.10 F.

findings.claim: In a one-generation simulator built from these measurements, the recheck's lives are 1.7-5.6x less productive than first-pass lives. Two kinds of saving exist. Keeping the same per-generation selection quality saves only 1.2-1.45x. Trading per-generation selection for more generations saves 2-3.4x per life. The second kind is risky because the late population sits near mutation-selection balance.
findings.evidence: analyze_noise.py: a nonparametric empirical-Bayes prior (NPMLE) fitted to the 256 candidates, per-genome residual bootstrap, shared life effects for CRN, and a sensitivity term tau for hidden small effects. S = true-mean selection differential of the 32 chosen. The table compares each scheme with the pilot (1024 lives), at tau 0.1-0.2 for speck and 0.1 for catch. One life each for 256 genomes (256 lives): S 79-84% (speck) and 60% (catch); 3.1-3.3x and 2.4x S per life. 256 x 1 then top 64 x 3 (448 lives): 91-94% and 80%; 2.1x and 1.85x. 256 x 1, top 128 +1, top 64 +2 (512 lives): 93-95% and 86%; 1.9x and 1.7x. 256 x 3 with no recheck (768 lives): 91-94% and 84%; 1.2x and 1.1x. 256 x 2 then top 64 x 5 (832 lives): 98-99% and 96%; 1.2x. lam 480, 1 life, top 64 x 3 (704 lives): 98-101% and 89%; 1.4x and 1.3x. lam 480 with three stages (768 lives): 100-103% and 96%; 1.3x. lam 992 at 1 life is worse than the pilot at equal cost. Pooling the parents' previous 7 lives adds under 2% to S. Marginal S per 1,000 recheck lives vs first-pass lives: 0.078 vs 0.434 in speck, 0.10 vs 0.17 in catch. Caveat: children lose 0.47 F (speck) or 0.10 F (catch) to mutation, while the pilot's S is about 0.35-0.45 and 0.16, and valid F rose only about 0.006 F per generation after gen 300. A lower S per generation could lower the plateau unless the mutation load also falls. This one-generation model ignores drift and diversity.

findings.claim: Short lives (T=512) give about 1.2-1.4x more selection information per CPU-second than T=1024. They change what is selected, though. In SPECK they predict T=1024 performance on independent lives about as well as T=1024 itself; in catch_v1 they do so worse. Shortening T only in early generations would save at most about 5%.
findings.evidence: 256 candidates x 4 lives at T=512, on the same seeds as T=1024 (each T=512 life is the first half of the T=1024 life). speck s5: CPU per life 0.088 vs 0.165 s, noise variance 6.74 vs 4.30, information per CPU 1.19x. Spearman with T=1024 on the same lives is 0.70; as a predictor of T=1024 on the other 12 lives it is 0.20, against 0.195 for T=1024 itself. It finds 83% of the bottom 5%. Bodies are already at 123 cells by T/2. catch_v1 s5: information per CPU 1.44x, prediction of T=1024 on other lives 0.13 vs 0.23, bottom-5% recall 58%. Generations with median body under 30 cells use about 5% of generation time (3.4 of 68.8 h). Load bias: T512 and T1024 chunks ran in different load windows; CPU per life varied about 20% between windows.

findings.claim: Early-stopping doomed lives is worth little late in a run, but founder sampling is dominated by guard-tripping lives. Capping n_max at 256 for founder lives cuts founder CPU 4x and leaves the chosen founders unchanged. Founder 'earners' on 2 lives are mostly luck.
findings.evidence: Late populations had 0 extinct and 0 guard lives in 4,096 (speck), 4,096 (catch) and 5,120 (2-cell) lives. In the logs, body generations have pop_guard 0.4-0.5% of lives. CPU per life is about the same for every genome (speck children 0.189 vs parents 0.176 CPU-s), so broken children cost 4-10% of candidate CPU. Founders: batch 0 of speck s5 reproduced exactly (layout.random(1024) on the run's own 2 lives). Guard lives are 32% of lives but hold 81% of events. With n_max 256, CPU falls from 123.6 to 30.7 s and events by 4.8x; the top 8, the earner set (4) and every earner's F are identical; earners peak at 45 cells or fewer. The 4 earners on the run's own lives earn on none of 2 fresh lives (top-8 mean F 0.067 on own lives vs -0.062 on fresh). Founders are 4.6% of pilot time but 50-70% of the wall time of the runs stuck at 1-2 cells. File: samples/founders/speck_lmax4_hexprism_sex_s5/founders.json.

findings.claim: How load biases the measurements.
findings.evidence: Everything ran under nice 19 at load average 15-57 on 14 threads (the pilot plus many niced sibling jobs). CPU-s per life for 120-cell speck bodies was 0.15-0.25 (1.6-2.4 us per event); catch 75-cell bodies 0.10-0.14 (1.2-1.3 us per event); 2-cell bodies 0.0016; founders 0.06 (0.015 capped). Contention for SMT and E-cores and frequency drops inflate these by an unknown factor, likely 1.3-2x against an idle machine. Savings given as lives per generation, the variance decompositions and the selection simulations do not depend on load. Wall-time splits from the pilot logs are inflated about uniformly.

recommendations.change: Keep common random numbers (shared life seeds and T within a generation and its recheck). They are already implemented; do not count on them for more savings late in a run.
recommendations.expected_gain: None beyond today. They are worth 1.1-1.6x in lives late in a run and 7-13x in the 1-2 cell regime, where they are what makes selection work.
recommendations.preserves_exactness: Yes. This is the current behaviour.
recommendations.risk: None.

recommendations.change: Monitoring cadence: run clone forks every 50 generations instead of 10, and possibly valid/held-out every 20.
recommendations.expected_gain: About 3% of run compute. Clone and fork lives are about 26k per run, against 512k selection plus recheck lives.
recommendations.preserves_exactness: Yes for the evolution. Valid, held-out and clone lives use their own hash seeds and never touch the torch generator, so the selection trajectory stays bitwise identical. Only the logged monitoring rows change.
recommendations.risk: Coarser time resolution of msg_reliance, sense_reliance and valid F curves.

recommendations.change: Founder sampling: give founder lives their own live-cell guard (n_max 256). Optionally make the search two-stage: 16,384 genomes x 1 capped life, then the top 256 x 4 more lives, then the top 8.
recommendations.expected_gain: The cap cuts founder CPU 4x: about 3.5% of a body run, about 2x for runs that get stuck at 1-2 cells. The two-stage search brings founders to about 16% of today's founder compute (about 6x) and picks founders that also earn on fresh lives.
recommendations.preserves_exactness: No. This changes the algorithm: capped founder lives score the guard charge, and the two-stage search changes which founders are picked. In the 1,024-genome test the top 8 and the earner set were unchanged by the cap. Needs a founder-only world override in evolve_life; a global world.n_max would also cap selection lives, where bodies reach 190-270 cells.
recommendations.risk: A founder that legitimately exceeds 256 cells would be lost; earners in the test peaked at 45 cells.

recommendations.change: Drop or adapt the recheck. Option a: evolve.recheck_k=0. Option b: switch the recheck off automatically once the logged shortlist Spearman (F_base vs F_recheck, already in lineage.jsonl) stays near 0 for about 20 generations.
recommendations.expected_gain: 1.33x fewer lives per generation (the recheck is 22% of compute). Per-generation S stays at 91-94% (speck) or 84% (catch) of the pilot.
recommendations.preserves_exactness: No. This changes the algorithm, and selection trajectories are not comparable with the pilot. Option a is config-only.
recommendations.risk: Slightly more broken parents get through (0.7 vs 0.3 of 32 per generation in speck). The recheck's protective role for small bodies early on (recheck_bodies) would need checking for option a.

recommendations.change: Same selection quality per generation, cheaper. Option 1: life.lives=2, evolve.recheck_lives=5 (256 x 2, then top 64 x 5; config-only). Option 2: race a larger brood with evolve.lam=480, life.lives=1, recheck_k=64, recheck_lives=3 (config-only); a third stage (top 128 +1, then top 64 +2) needs a small code change.
recommendations.expected_gain: Option 1: 832 lives, 1.23x fewer, keeping 96-99% of the pilot's S in both worlds. Option 2: 704 lives, 1.45x fewer, 98-101% of S in speck and 89% in catch; the three-stage version uses 768 lives (1.33x fewer) and keeps 96-103%.
recommendations.preserves_exactness: No. This changes the algorithm (selection scheme); config overrides only, no kernel or ABI change.
recommendations.risk: Low. The one-generation model ignores drift and diversity. lam 480 doubles lineage and breeding work, which is small next to the kernel.

recommendations.change: Fixed compute, more generations: one life per genome. Either 256 x 1 with no recheck (life.lives=1, recheck_k=0), or 256 x 1 then top 64 x 3 (life.lives=1, recheck_lives=3). Spend the saved compute on 2.3-4x more generations or more seeds.
recommendations.expected_gain: Lives per generation fall 4x (256) or 2.3x (448). S per life rises 2.4-3.3x for 1 life or 1.7-2.2x for the halving variant. For the pilot's 500 generations, the halving variant would cut about 71.7 h of process time to about 35 h.
recommendations.preserves_exactness: No. This changes the algorithm; config-only.
recommendations.risk: High. Per-generation S falls to 60-84% (one life) or 80-94% (halving) of the pilot, while each generation's children lose 0.10-0.47 F to mutation. Near mutation-selection balance this can lower the plateau, so it must be A/B tested at equal compute first (idle_ab_selection.sh). Pairing it with a lower mutation load (n_mut 1 or smaller sigma) is a natural follow-up.

recommendations.change: Do not reuse parent evaluations across generations, and do not raise lambda at one life without a recheck stage.
recommendations.expected_gain: Pooling parents' previous lives adds under 2% to S. Skipping parent re-evaluation would save at most 9.4% of lives, but would freeze parents' winner's-curse inflation (+1.3 to 1.6 F in speck). lam 992 at one life costs the same as the pilot and gives 88-100% of its S in speck (50-73% in catch).
recommendations.preserves_exactness: Yes. Keeping the current behaviour.
recommendations.risk: None.

recommendations.change: Shorter selection lives, for example T_choices [512, 768] instead of [768, 1024, 1536]. Do not bother with an early-generation-only T schedule.
recommendations.expected_gain: T=512 lives cost 0.53x as much and carry 1.2-1.4x more information per CPU-second, so the selection phase would need about 1.6-2x less compute for equal information. Early generations are only about 5% of time, so an early-only schedule saves at most about 2.5%.
recommendations.preserves_exactness: No. This changes the objective: GB11 drew T up to 1536 to keep selection pressure on late-life growth and stop rules.
recommendations.risk: Medium to high. In catch_v1, T=512 predicts T=1024 performance on independent lives worse (Spearman 0.13 vs 0.23), and it relaxes the pressure GB11 was added for.

recommendations.change: Do not build kernel-side early termination or surrogates for doomed lives.
recommendations.expected_gain: At most 2-5% in body generations: no extinct or guard lives in the late populations, a pop_guard of 0.4-0.5%, and broken children are 4-10% of CPU.
recommendations.preserves_exactness: Would change the kernel ABI and F for stopped lives.
recommendations.risk: Not worth the ABI and verification cost.

recommendations.change: Design question for the user (reward variance). Selection noise is Poisson noise in the capture count. A denser auxiliary signal (time in the capture zone or click distance, both already in the ledger as measurement-only zone_samples and dist_sum) would cut the noise per life.
recommendations.expected_gain: Potentially large: capture noise is about 100% of per-life variance. Not quantified here.
recommendations.preserves_exactness: No. This is reward shaping and changes the objective; cells would still not sense it.
recommendations.risk: High. It selects for a proxy, and a fitness term should be justified as a necessary fixed rule.
