verdict.title: Review of the selection-efficiency report: the measurements hold up, but it scores schemes with the wrong metric, so the claimed recheck and one-life savings mostly disappear

checks.claim: Compute split: selection 69%, recheck 22%, monitoring and overhead 4%, founders 4.6%, final 0.2%. 95% of generation time falls in generations whose median body has at least 30 cells.
checks.recheck: Wrote my own script (verify/split.py) over all 29 curves.jsonl and the 28 finished results.jsonl. The pilot has moved on since the report was written: speck s9 is at generation 145. I also read evolve.py to see exactly what t_eval, t_recheck and t_gen time.
checks.result: Selection 53.5 h (67.9%), recheck 17.5 h (22.2%), rest 3.2 h (4.1%), founders 4.4 h (5.6%), final 0.17 h (0.2%), out of 78.8 process-hours. 95.3% of generation time is in generations with median_n >= 30 (70.8 of 74.3 h). Late generations spend 0.31-0.38 as long on the recheck as on selection, against a lives ratio of 256/768 = 0.33, so recheck lives cost about the same as first-pass lives. In the body runs, Python overhead outside the kernel is 0.02 s per generation (0.07% of t_gen), so serial per-generation overhead does not limit anything. The 'rest' share is almost all the every-10-generation monitoring (4.2-4.7% of t_gen). Founders take 50-71% of the wall time of runs stuck at 1-2 cells. These are wall-clock seconds under load, but every phase shares the same load, so the split holds.

checks.claim: Inside the shortlist, Spearman(F_base, F_recheck) has a median of about 0.03, and 0.00-0.017 at generations >= 450. Parents kept: 4-6. Parents in the shortlist: 8-10.
checks.recheck: Recomputed from lineage.jsonl with my own code (verify/lineage_check.py, numpy rank correlation), using only generations whose median_n >= 30.
checks.result: Median rho is 0.026 over 6,298 body generations (mean 0.031 +- 0.003); at generations >= 450 it is 0.016. Every body run has a median of 4-6 parents kept (mostly 5), 8-10 parents in the shortlist and recheck_changed 8-12. If the 8.5% broken children drop out and the rest are exchangeable, you would expect 8.6 parents in the shortlist and 4.3 kept, which matches.

checks.claim: Per-life F noise in SPECK is Poisson noise in the capture count (R_cap/T = 0.49 F per capture, about 19 captures at T 1024, per-life sd about 2.0 F). catch_v1's per-life sd is 0.62.
checks.recheck: Ran my own kernel lives (verify/noise_check.py, scratch kernel build, threads=2, nice 19) on 64 fresh seeds from a block the agent did not use (51000000+). Bodies: the best genome of speck s5 and of lmax4 s5, both at T=1024.
checks.result: Speck s5 best: F 6.37 +- 0.29, per-life sd 2.33, 18.9 captures, corr(F, captures) 0.990, slope 0.46 F per capture (R_cap/T = 0.488), residual variance 0.11 of 5.42. Capture dispersion is 1.32, against 1.0 for Poisson; one genome on 64 lives cannot separate these. catch s5 best: sd 0.60, 49.6 captures, dispersion 0.94, corr 0.89; Poisson capture noise predicts a variance of 0.47 against 0.36 measured. Capture count drives the per-life noise in both worlds; calling it Poisson exactly is approximate. CPU: 0.25 CPU-s per life (2.7 us per event) for speck and 0.16 (1.5 us per event) for catch, at load average 23-28, so inflated.

checks.claim: Capping founder lives at n_max 256 cuts founder CPU about 4x and leaves the chosen founders unchanged (tested on batch 0).
checks.recheck: Reproduced a different batch, batch 1 (the run generator's second layout.random(1024) draw, on the run's own batch-1 founder lives), at base n_max and at 256 (verify/founder_cap.py). I also checked the founder event of every run and read sample_founders and the guard charge code.
checks.result: CPU fell from 125.0 to 23.8 s (5.3x) and events from 93.2M to 19.5M (4.8x). Event counts do not depend on load. The top 8 is identical. Batch 1 has no earners, though, so this batch cannot test whether the earner set survives the cap. Every founder run found 8 or more earners among its 16,384 genomes, so the cap changes the selection only if an earner grows past 256 cells. It also cuts the guard charge (c_live x n_max x remaining time) by 4x. The cap needs a founder-only override in code: cfg.world applies to every life.

checks.claim: Recheck lives are 1.7-5.6x less productive than first-pass lives (marginal S per 1,000 lives: 0.078 vs 0.434 in speck, 0.10 vs 0.17 in catch).
checks.recheck: Recomputed from the agent's own simulator output (runs/*/noise.json, schemes) as differences between schemes (verify/marginal.txt).
checks.result: Wrong comparison. 0.434 and 0.173 are the AVERAGE S per 1k lives of the 256x3 first pass (S/768), while 0.078 and 0.10 are MARGINAL values. At the margin, at tau 0.1, a recheck life adds 0.076 (speck) or 0.103 (catch) per 1k, while a third first-pass life adds 0.052 or 0.060 and a fourth adds 0.031 or 0.041. At every tau, recheck lives are 1.2-2.0x MORE productive than a third first-pass life, and about equal to a second one. The same holds for D.

checks.claim: Dropping the recheck keeps 91-94% of S (speck) and 84% (catch) for 1.33x fewer lives. One life per genome gives 2.4-3.3x S per life. lam 480 keeps 98-101% of S at 1.45x fewer lives.
checks.recheck: Read analyze_noise.simulate. S is the chosen mean minus the mean of the scheme's own candidate pool, so it includes the children's mutation load, which is roughly the same for every scheme. It also flatters larger broods, whose pool mean is lower. The quantity that adds up over generations is D = chosen mean minus current parents' mean. The agent's simulator already computes D (delta_parents) but the report never uses it. I tabulated D from noise.json, and as an independent check I wrote my own parametric simulator (verify/sel_sim.py, sel_sim_D.py).
checks.result: In D, speck at tau 0.1-0.26 and catch at tau 0-0.15: no recheck keeps 65-78% of per-generation gain at 0.87-1.04x gain per life, so it saves nothing per unit of progress. 256x1 keeps 14-44% at 0.54-1.76x. lam480 x1 >64+3 keeps 67-81% at 0.97-1.17x. Halving 256x1 >64+3 keeps 62-73% at 1.42-1.66x. 256x2 >64+5 keeps 92-98% at 1.14-1.21x. lam96 x3 >64x4 keeps 80-93% at 1.29-1.49x; the report missed this one. My parametric model with the report's own speck numbers even gives negative D for the pilot, so the result is very sensitive to the model.

checks.claim: The one-generation simulator's gains carry over to evolution, with the caveat that it ignores drift and diversity.
checks.recheck: Compared the simulator's predicted per-generation gain for the pilot with the progress the pilot actually made: the slope of valid F over generations >= 300 in the 14 finished body runs (verify/progress.py).
checks.result: Predicted pilot D is 0.054-0.167 F per generation (speck) and 0.047-0.157 (catch). The actual valid-F slope has a median of 0.005 F per generation (range 0.0003-0.018). The model overpredicts progress by about 10-30x: it redraws standing variation every generation, which real selection uses up. The ranking of schemes might survive, but none of its ratios can be trusted without a real A/B.

checks.claim: Running clone forks every 50 generations instead of 10 saves about 3% and leaves the evolution bitwise identical.
checks.recheck: Read evolve_life, clones.run_forks, clone_targets and LifeEvaluator.draw, and counted fork lives. Measured the extra time of monitoring generations (verify/overhead.py).
checks.result: Each clone event is 8 genomes x 3 times x (1 twin + 6 conditions) x 3 seeds = 504 full lives; valid plus held-out add 40-46. Monitoring is 4.2-4.7% of t_gen, and clones are about 92% of those lives, so going to every 50 saves about 3.2%. Valid, held-out and clone lives use hash-keyed draws, clone_targets is deterministic, and none of them touches the torch generator, so selection stays bitwise identical.

checks.claim: Shorter selection lives (T_choices [512, 768]) are a small, config-only change.
checks.recheck: Read the guard at the top of evolve_life.
checks.result: evolve_life raises ValueError unless life.T is one of T_choices. With life.T at 1024, T_choices [512, 768] crashes, so life.T must also change. That changes the length of the valid, held-out, final and clone lives as well, so the reported F is no longer comparable with the pilot's. In catch_v1, T=512 also predicts T=1024 worse (0.13 against 0.23).

checks.claim: In the idle A/B script, the arms get equal lives, and valid and clones every 10 generations add about 5% to every arm alike. Cost: about 7 CPU-hours per arm and seed, about 2 h on a 64-vCPU machine.
checks.recheck: Read idle_ab_selection.sh and ab_configs. Worked out monitoring lives per arm, and checked the cost against speck s5's late t_gen.
checks.result: Monitoring is fixed per generation (544 lives every 10 generations), not per life. It is about 5% of the pilot arm's selection lives but 20% for ab_L1, 11% for L1rc3, 6% for L2rc5 and 7% for lam480. Because the comparison uses cumulative t_gen, the cheaper arms are penalised by up to about 14%. Set clones.every=0 in every arm. The test is also underpowered: at the real progress rate (0.005 F per generation), the pilot arm gains about 0.75 F over 150 generations, while one run's final F on 64 lives has an SE of about 0.25-0.3 F. With 3 seeds per arm, gaps of 0.2-0.3 F between arms are below the noise. Cost: late speck s5 generations take 93 s of wall time at 3 threads under load, so 150 generations is about 11.6 thread-hours loaded, roughly 6-9 CPU-hours idle. The 7 CPU-hour figure is plausible, but with 15 runs in one wave, wall time on a 64-vCPU (SMT) machine is more like 2-4 h than 2 h.

verdict.corrected_recommendations:
These are ranked by value per unit of effort. Gains are recomputed by me. 'D' is the per-generation gain in the parents' true mean, the quantity that adds up over generations. All selection-scheme numbers come from the agent's one-generation model, which overpredicts real progress by 10-30x, so treat them as hypotheses until the A/B is done.

1. Run clone forks every 50 generations instead of every 10 (clones.every=50; config only). This saves about 3.2% of generation time and leaves evolution bitwise identical. The cost is coarser msg_reliance and sense_reliance curves. Leave valid and held-out at every 10: together they are only about 0.4%.

2. Give founder lives their own cap of n_max 256. This needs a small code change, a founder-only world override in evolve_life or sample_founders. Founder CPU drops 4-5x (I measured 5.3x CPU and 4.8x events on batch 1; the agent measured 4x on batch 0), and the top 8 were the same in both batches. That is about 4.5% of total pilot compute (founders are now 5.6%) and about 2x for runs stuck at 1-2 cells, which are cheap anyway. It is not exact: the guard charge shrinks 4x, and an earner that grows past 256 cells would be lost. Optionally, make the founder search two-stage: 16,384 x 1 capped life, then the top 256 x 4. Founder compute falls to about 13-16% of today's, and the 2-life earners already look like luck.

3. Keep common random numbers and the re-evaluation of parents. This is the current behaviour, so it costs nothing.

4. Before changing selection, run an equal-compute A/B with three fixes: clones.every=0 in every arm, 6-8 seeds per arm instead of 3, and judging on valid-F slope plus at least 256 final lives. The cheaper world (catch_v1) can serve as the second test. The candidates, in their D per life from the agent's own model:
   - (a) 256x2 then top 64 x5 (life.lives=2, recheck_lives=5; config only): 1.14-1.21x per life, keeps 92-98% of per-generation D. Lowest risk.
   - (b) Successive halving, 256x1 then top 64 x3 (life.lives=1, recheck_lives=3; config only): 1.42-1.66x per life, but only 62-73% of per-generation D. That is risky near mutation-selection balance.
   - (c) A smaller brood, lam 96 with 3 lives then top 64 x4 (640 lives): 1.29-1.49x per life at 80-93% of D. The report missed it. It reduces diversity.
   - (d) lam 480 x1 then top 64 x3: 0.97-1.17x per life, 67-81% of D. Not worth it.

5. Do not drop the recheck, and do not use 1 life with no recheck. Dropping the recheck saves 1.33x in lives per generation, but per-generation D falls to 65-78%, so D per life is 0.87-1.04x: nothing saved per unit of progress. The report's claim that recheck lives are 1.7-5.6x less productive compared marginal values with averages; at the margin, recheck lives beat a third first-pass life. One life with no recheck keeps only 14-44% of D.

6. Shorter lives (T_choices [512, 768]) are not config-only: life.T must also change, which changes every judged life. The objective changes, catch_v1 evidence is negative, and GB11's reasoning argues against it. Low priority.

7. Kernel-side early stopping of doomed lives: agreed, not worth it (2-5% at most, plus ABI and verification cost).

8. A design question for the user, with potentially the largest payoff: about 80-99% of per-life variance is capture-count noise. A denser fitness signal (the zone_samples and dist_sum ledger columns) could cut the lives needed several-fold, but it changes the objective and has to be justified as a necessary fixed rule.
verdict.missed:
1. The report's headline metric is wrong. S is measured against each scheme's own candidate pool, so it includes the children's mutation load, which is much the same for every scheme and compresses the differences between them. It also flatters larger broods, whose pool mean is lower. The agent's own simulator outputs D (delta_parents), and D reverses the conclusions on the recheck and on one-life selection.

2. The one-generation model predicts 0.05-0.17 F of progress per generation for the pilot. The pilot's actual late progress is a median of 0.005 F per generation. A model that is off by this much cannot support savings estimates; only the A/B can.

3. The A/B as written gives the cheaper arms up to about 14% extra monitoring overhead and is statistically underpowered (see checks).

4. Sample efficiency is not where the rental question gets decided. The pilot's work is already embarrassingly parallel across runs. Serial Python overhead is 0.02 s per generation (0.07% of t_gen in body runs), so on a rented machine the way to scale is more concurrent runs (seeds or arms) at 2-4 threads each. Schemes with fewer lives per generation (256-448 lives per kernel call, two synchronous calls per generation) leave each run less to spread over threads, so they make per-run thread scaling worse.

5. Lower-noise worlds are cheaper to test in. Per-life sd is 2.0-2.3 F in speck against about 0.6 in catch_v1, which matters when sizing any A/B.

6. Load bias in my own numbers: CPU per life (0.25 s speck, 0.16 s catch) was measured at load average 23-28 and is inflated. The founder events ratio (4.8x) and every lives-based ratio do not depend on load.

My scripts and outputs are in /tmp/claude-1000/-home-jgon-project-ml-cell-dev/aefb0c66-3af5-49c4-936c-154d6434706c/scratchpad/compute/samples/verify/: split.py, lineage_check.py, noise_check.py, founder_cap.py, sel_sim.py, sel_sim_D.py, marginal.txt, overhead.py, progress.py, and out/noise_*.json and out/founders_*.json.

report.title: Scale-out and rental options for cell-dev evolution: workload, per-core speed, GPU fit, prices (2026-10-09), costs of 3 experiments, and what to change before renting

findings.claim: So far the pilot has used about 189 laptop-CPU-hours (a laptop-CPU-hour, written L-h, is one CPU-hour on this laptop under pilot load). That is 72.6 run-hours of wall time, or 218 thread-slot-hours at 3 threads. About 217 L-h and about 83 run-hours are projected when it finishes, roughly 24 h of elapsed time on 4 job slots. This is close to run_catch_pilot.sh's 'high' estimate of 86 job-hours.
findings.evidence: pilot_compute.py reads only outputs/catch_pilot/*: results.jsonl wall_s, curves.jsonl t_gen/t_eval/t_recheck, and /proc of the live src.run processes. 28 of 29 runs have started, 24 are done, 12,512 generations so far, and the sweep has been running 65,409 s (18.2 h). CPU time was measured directly for the 4 running 3-thread jobs from /proc utime+stime: 2.57, 2.58, 2.62 and 2.64 CPU-s per wall-s. That ratio was applied to finished runs, because the pilot records only wall time. Still to run: lmax4_s9 104 gens, speck s6/s7/s8 46/53/85 gens, about 14 L-h together, plus speck_lmax4_s9, which has not started (about 14 L-h, range 5-26). Raw numbers are in scaleout/pilot_compute.json. Load bias: the machine runs at load 24-30 (sometimes 37-130 from other users' jobs). That inflates wall time about 13% over CPU time, and per-thread CPU time about 1.5-2x over an idle laptop.

findings.claim: Cost differs about 50x between run types. Stuck runs (1-3 cells) cost 0.5-1.0 L-h each, and about two thirds of that is founder sampling. Grown 500-generation runs cost 6-26 L-h, and the SPECK L4 arm uses more than half of the pilot.
findings.evidence: pilot_compute.json gives these figures (wall hours at 3 threads -> L-h). Stuck runs (8: lmax2 s0/s1, lmax4 s0-s4/s7): 0.21-0.37 h -> 0.54-0.96 L-h, with founders taking 530-950 s wall (16,384 genomes x 2 lives). Grown lmax4/lmax2 runs: 1.3-4.1 h -> 3.4-10.6 L-h. Seeded runs (300 gens): 1.1-3.1 h -> 2.9-8.0 L-h. SPECK L4 (500 gens): done runs 0.8-6.9 h (2.2-18 L-h), running runs at 8.3 h and growing (projected 25 L-h). Totals by arm: speck_lmax4 115 L-h so far (about 140 projected), lmax4 32.7, speck_seeded 16.6, seeded 13.7, lmax2 11.4. Late generations take 0.86 s in stuck runs and 40-115 s in runs with bodies of 60-170 cells.

findings.claim: The cost of a generation is set by body size. A good model is CPU-s ≈ T x (1.12e-3 x population mean body + 0.29e-3 x best body), which is about 1.46 us of laptop CPU per selection cell-time unit. At ~120-cell bodies a generation costs about 194 L-s, and 1000 generations cost about 54 L-h per run. The kernel is about 95% of every generation. Python bookkeeping takes about 0.06 s per generation.
findings.evidence: Least-squares fit over 11,339 plain generation rows of all pilot runs (fit_gen_cost.py -> fit_gen_cost.json). Generations with a valid/held-out/clone round cost 41% more, which adds about 4% when spread over the 10 generations. Cross-check: speck_s5's last 50 generations took 222 L-s (body 120) and speck_s6's took 298 L-s (body 169). In stuck runs, t_gen - t_eval - t_recheck is 0.06 s per generation. Rule of thumb: about 1.6 L-s per cell of mean body per generation.

findings.claim: The single-thread kernel costs about 1.25-1.41 us of CPU per cell-unit on both P- and E-cores under load, and 2.76 us on the low-power E-cores. Cost per event, about 1.6-2.1 us or 4.2-5.2k cycles, is the stable figure. CATCH v1 bodies cost about twice as much per cell-unit as SPECK bodies because they produce 1.31 events per cell-unit against 0.73-0.80.
findings.evidence: bench_cell.py bench pinned to one CPU (os.sched_setaffinity), with the core clock sampled from scaling_cur_freq. Test body: speck_lmax4_hexprism_sex_s5, 16 lives, T=1024, n_end 119. Results: cpu6 (E) 1.245 us at 2.70 GHz = 3.36 kcycles/cu; cpu9 (E) 1.364 us at 2.51 GHz; cpu0/cpu2 (P thread with a busy HT sibling) 1.30/1.41 us at 3.19/2.92 GHz = 4.1 kcycles/cu; cpu12 (LP-E) 2.76 us at 1.42 GHz. In verify runs, lmax4_hexprism_sex_s5 (catch_v1_l4) costs 2.4-2.7 us/cu. No hardware counters were available (perf_event_paranoid=4), so cycles are CPU time x sampled clock. The pinned core was shared with pilot threads, so cache contention inflates these numbers. Files: bench_laptop_cpu{0,2,6,9,12}_t1.json, measurements.json.

findings.claim: Runs are embarrassingly parallel. Generations are a strict serial chain. Lives inside a generation are independent and give bitwise-identical results at any thread count, but each generation has only 768 selection lives and 256 recheck lives. That makes up to about 32 threads per run efficient. Past that, a big box should run many runs side by side.
findings.evidence: In evolve_life, selection at generation g sets the parents of g+1, which is a barrier. LifeEvaluator splits genomes into chunks of 256 (evolve.batch), and 256 genomes x 3 lives = 768 lives go into one life_run call. The recheck adds 64 x 4 = 256 lives, and every 10 generations there are also 16 valid lives, 24 held-out lives and the clone forks. Founders are 32,768 lives in calls of 512. The kernel uses '#pragma omp parallel for schedule(dynamic,1)' over lives. Efficiency model at 120 cells (per generation: 200 L-s of work + 0.15 L-s Python + about 0.3 L-s of dynamic-schedule tail): 97% at 12 threads, 96.5% at 16, 93% at 32, 87% at 64, 70% at 192 (gen_eff_120cells.txt). In verify, threads 1 and 2 gave identical hashes for all 18 lives.

findings.claim: Memory and data are not constraints. A job peaks at about 0.43 GB, and inputs and outputs are a few MB per run.
findings.evidence: VmHWM of the 4 pilot jobs is 420-427 MB, and current RSS is 70-130 MB. RESULTS.md reports 0.29-0.72 GB for gate runs. At 40-100 jobs, a 192-vCPU box needs 20-45 GB, so compute-optimized or highcpu shapes are enough. Inputs: repo 8.4 MB plus a 4.5 MB .git, plus pip wheels. Outputs: 5-9 MB per 500-generation run (lineage.jsonl 4.7 MB, clones.jsonl 3.5 MB), 202 MB for the whole pilot plus 15 MB of logs. Egress for an experiment costs well under $1.

GB6 single-core: c7a 1,984, hpc7a 1,998, c3d 2,024, c7i 2,055, c8a 2,816, Hetzner CCX63 1,859. PassMark single-thread: c7a 2,887, c7i 3,024, c8a 3,816. A loaded laptop thread is about 900-1,000 GB6-equivalent: the roughly 2,500 P-core score scaled to 2.6-3 GHz and to HT or E-core sharing. A 1.25x SMT gain is assumed (range 1.1-1.4). AWS says c7a and c8a have no SMT ('each vCPU is a physical core'), and c8a is about 30% faster than c7a. The kernel's working set (Cell struct about 1.2 KB x cells, plus sites, inboxes, heap and records) is a few hundred KB, which suits the L2/L3 of these servers. To be measured on the box with bench_cell.py fleet (us_per_cu_per_vcpu against the laptop's 1.3-1.46).

findings.claim: A GPU port would not help. The kernel is a sequential, branchy, exact discrete-event simulation per life. A generation has too few lives to fill a GPU, warps would diverge across event types, and the bitwise contract would break unless both CPU and GPU switched to a common software libm (a new ABI, with every hash changing). A time-stepped approximation would break the clockless exact design.
findings.evidence: kernel.c: each life has its own binary heap of events (HEnt/hpush/hpop) and per-site time-ordered batches. One sequential accountant consumes records in canonical (t, sitekey, seq) order. Cells live in an open-addressing hash map, pools grow by realloc, footprints use union-find, and records use merge sorts. The code is FP64 and calls glibc exp/log/pow (GLIBC_2.29 versions), sincos, tanh, nearbyint and llround (nm -D of the built .so). It costs about 4.2-5.2k cycles per event and 0.15-0.3 s of CPU per life at 120-170 cells. With 768-1024 lives per generation, one life per GPU thread gives about 24-32 warps on an H100's 132 SMs, under 1% occupancy. Even 100 runs batched in lockstep would leave in-order, divergent per-thread code with spilled state running about 50-100x slower than a CPU core per thread. The best case after months of rewriting is roughly tens to a few hundred CPU-core equivalents per GPU. A 192-core spot box gives that for $3-6/h with no rewrite.

findings.claim: src/run.py cannot resume a run. Any preemption or crash restarts the run from generation 0, and rerunning scripts/sweep.py overwrites every run in its matrix. Exact resume is cheap to add: the torch.Generator is the only random state in a run.
findings.evidence: main_life opens curves.jsonl with 'w'. Lineage opens lineage.jsonl and clones.jsonl with 'w'. evolve_life keeps pop/ids/breeds/origins/next_id/next_innov/evals/rc_lives in memory, and population.json is written only after the last generation. sweep.py has no skip or resume and launches every run. Life seeds, the T draw and envelope draws are spec.hash64 values of (seed, purpose, index, life) (evaluate.life_seed, LifeEvaluator.draw), and the kernel is stateless. Breeding, mutation and founder sampling use one torch.Generator, and get_state/set_state restores it exactly. A sketch is in scaleout/resume_sketch.py.

findings.claim: Bitwise results on another machine are likely but need checking. The kernel calls glibc libm functions, which use FMA variants chosen at load time on x86-64. Breeding runs through torch's CPU kernels, and an AVX-512 server picks different kernels from this AVX2 laptop. requirements.txt is not pinned. alt-arcs' Modal image (debian_slim) ships an older glibc than the laptop's.

The kernel .so imports exp@GLIBC_2.29, log@GLIBC_2.29, pow@GLIBC_2.29, sincos, tanh, frexp, ldexp, llround, nearbyint, nextafter and floor. requirements.txt says torch>=2.2, numpy>=1.26. genome.py draws torch.randn/rand for mutations and crossover. The C kernel should be built into the image, and Volume commits should be periodic. Without resume, Modal's restart-on-preemption reruns a run from generation 0.
findings.evidence: ../alt-arcs/src/modal_app.py: debian_slim with python 3.12, add_local_dir of the repo, gpu=A10G, timeout 6 h, Volume at /data, sweep.py run as a subprocess, volume.commit at the end. Sketch: scaleout/modal_cell_dev.py (ubuntu:24.04 + add_python 3.12, pinned wheels, build.build() at image build time, cpu=8 with 16 threads, retries=2, commits every 5 min, starmap over sweep.matrix()). git_state() returns None in an image without .git.

recommendations.change: Add exact checkpoint/resume to life-mode runs. Every ~5 generations, save pop, ids, breeds, origins, next_id, next_innov, evals, rc_lives, valid, heldout, chosen.fitness, curves, the founders info, torch.Generator.get_state(), accumulated wall time, and the byte offsets of curves/lineage/clones.jsonl, written atomically (tmp file + os.replace). On resume: truncate the files to those offsets, reopen them with 'a', and continue at g+1. Add logging.resume=true, and add sweep.py --skip-done, --resume and --shard i/n. See scaleout/resume_sketch.py.
recommendations.expected_gain: Makes spot and preemptible capacity safe: c7a, c3d or c8a spot is 45-65% cheaper than on-demand, and Modal preemptible is 3x cheaper than non-preemptible. Losing a ~5-hour run to a preemption drops from 100% of the run to at most 5 generations (a few minutes). A crashed or interrupted sweep also restarts without redoing finished runs.
recommendations.preserves_exactness: Yes, provided the generator state and all counters are restored. Life seeds and T draws are hashes of (seed, purpose, index), so a resumed run should match an uninterrupted one byte for byte except t_gen/t_eval/t_recheck/wall_s. A slow test should check this: 6 generations straight vs 3 + resume + 3, compared with replay_check.compare.
recommendations.risk: Low to medium. The main risk is missing a piece of state, for example a resume landing exactly at the final generation, or rows that only the 10th generations write. The split-vs-straight test catches this.

recommendations.change: Pin the environment and check determinism on every new machine type before a sweep. Pin exact versions (torch==2.14.1 from the CPU index, numpy==2.5.3, omegaconf==2.3.1, ...). Use an Ubuntu 24.04 base (glibc 2.39, gcc 13.3) rather than debian_slim. Set ATEN_CPU_CAPABILITY=avx2 so AVX-512 servers run the laptop's torch kernels. Then run bench_cell.py verify --reference verify_laptop.json and replay_check.py run/compare against replay_laptop_t2.

verdict.corrected_recommendations:
Ranked by value per unit of effort:

1. **Pin the environment and check bitwise portability before any rental.** Small effort; nothing rented is comparable to laptop runs without it.
   - Set `ATEN_CPU_CAPABILITY=avx2`. I showed directly that the torch.randn bits differ between CPU-dispatch levels (DEFAULT vs AVX2). Mutation noise and founder draws go through that path, and an AVX-512 server would pick yet another kernel.
   - Pin exact wheels and use the Ubuntu 24.04 image.
   - Optionally also pin numpy's SIMD level (X86_V3 here, X86_V4 on servers).
   - Run `bench_cell.py verify` and `replay_check.py` first on every machine type.

2. **Rent one many-core box for bursts, and do not rent GPUs.** Small effort, big value.
   - c8a.48xlarge at $5.54 spot, c7a spot at $3.40, or hpc7a on-demand at $7.20 (us-east-2) without resume. Prices are re-verified.
   - Rerunning the pilot takes about 1-1.2 h instead of about 28 h on the laptop, for about $6-16.
   - The 40-run x 1000-generation ablation takes about 4.5-5.5 h on one box, about $25-30 spot or $50-55 on-demand.
   - The speed factor (c8a about 2.6x the loaded laptop) is unverified. Spend the first 15 minutes on the box running `bench_cell.py fleet`.
   - One box is the better choice. A 5-box fleet is not about 1.1 h for $29: it is about 1.5 h and about $43, because the longest run is about 1.7x the mean, not 1.15x. Modal wall times are about 1.5x the report's (about 6 h for the ablation, same dollars).

3. **Choose the job layout, and add elastic threads (the latter was missed).** Small effort.
   - Keep the report's layout: one job per run, threads = ceil(1.5 x vCPU / runs) capped at 32, `OMP_WAIT_POLICY=PASSIVE`. My exact schedule simulation on measured life costs supports it: 95% efficiency at 32 threads, 89-91% at 64, 71-75% at 192.
   - New: let each kernel call use min(cap, free cores / running runs) threads instead of the fixed `cfg.threads`. Results do not depend on the thread count.
   - On one box this cuts the ablation from about 5.4 h to about 4.4 h.
   - On the laptop it removes tails like the current one: speck_lmax4_s9 will run alone on 3 of 14 threads for about 8 h, and would take about 2-2.5 h at 12 threads.
   - Also start the arms expected to run longest (SPECK L4) first.

4. **Checkpoint and resume, as the report specifies.** Medium effort.
   - This is what makes spot and preemptible capacity usable. c8a spot is 46% cheaper than on-demand, c7a spot 65%, and Modal preemptible 3x cheaper.
   - Against hpc7a on-demand, it saves about 40-50% per experiment, which is $15-70 at the sizes above. It is worth doing if you will rent more than a few times, or use Modal.
   - It also protects multi-hour laptop runs.
   - The state analysis is correct: the torch.Generator is the only RNG state.

5. **Record CPU time, host and CPU model, plus scheduler wait, in every row.** Small effort.
   - Also record run-queue wait (`/proc/self/task/*/schedstat`). On this laptop 11-15% of pilot thread time is spent waiting for a CPU, which getrusage alone cannot show.
   - Add the git fallback the report describes.

6. **Kernel build flags (missed).** Small effort, gain of at most about 5-10%, unresolved under this load.
   - -march=native, x86-64-v3, PGO and v3+PGO all gave all 5 hashes and the full ledger identical to the repo build on 16 lives.
   - Timings came out at 0.88-1.07x of the reference across two rounds, which is within the load noise.
   - Re-measure on an idle machine with `verify/variant_test.py` before changing `CFLAGS`.

7. **Merge or overlap the side evaluations run every 10th generation.** Medium effort, about 4% of CPU. Matters only at 32 or more threads per run. Do it after resume.

8. **Do not port to a GPU.** Agreed.
verdict.missed:
**1. Static threads leave tails, on the laptop now and on any rented box.**
- The pilot is in its tail right now: only speck_lmax4_s9 is running, at 3 threads, at generation 92. It already has 68-cell bodies, so it projects to about 20-25 L-h and about 8 h alone.
- That puts the pilot at about 225 L-h and about 28 h elapsed (the report said 217 and 24).
- `sweep.py` has fixed threads per job and FIFO order. Elastic per-call threads plus longest-first ordering are cheap fixes that keep results exact.

**2. The laptop is heavily shared, and that biases the L-h unit.**
- Load was 30-58 during this check. Pilot threads waited for a CPU 11-15% of their life.
- Recent generations ran 4-10x slower than normal (s6 generation 474: t_recheck 398 s against about 33 s).
- Wall times from the last hours are unreliable. The 'loaded laptop CPU-second' unit drifts with load, so calibrate on the rented box instead of trusting the conversion.

**3. Life cost is heavy-tailed, and per-event cost is not stable.**
- One child life in 256 had 8x the mean events but cost only about 2.5x the mean.
- Guard-tripping lives (0.3-1.5% of late genome-lives, n_max 1024 or e_max 5M events) were absent from my sample. They are what would hurt at 64 or more threads per run, which is another reason to cap at about 32.

**4. The fleet and Modal estimates assume the longest run is 1.15x the mean.**
- The pilot's SPECK L4 arm has max/mean 1.71.
- Fleet and Modal wall times, and fleet cost when boxes are billed until the last run ends, should be about 1.5x higher.
- One-box estimates move by 10% or less because of the 1.5x oversubscription.

**5. Where generation time goes is an experiment-design choice, not something to optimise silently.**
- The recheck is 25-30% of each generation (19.7 of 79 s in speck_s5 late; 32.6 of 108 s in s6).
- The T draw averages 1109, 8% over 1024.
- The side rounds add 4%.
- These are the largest software levers, but changing them changes the experiment, so they are the user's decision.

**6. The rent_box_setup.sh template can lose results.**
- It ends with `sudo shutdown -h now`. On a spot instance whose shutdown behaviour is 'terminate', the root volume and outputs are deleted unless they were synced.
- Set the instance-initiated shutdown behaviour to stop, or sync to S3 before shutdown.
- Also check spot interruption rates for 48xlarge pools (AWS Spot Advisor). I did not check them.
- c8a.48xlarge has 2 NUMA nodes. Pinning each run to one node (`numactl` or `taskset`) is a free tweak.

**7. The kernel was never profiled.**
- The report gives about 4-5k cycles per event, but no hotspot breakdown exists (perf is blocked here).
- A profile on the rented box (perf is usually allowed there) or with callgrind could find gains that multiply every rental dollar.
